What I heardFrom Richard Ladson · notes from our conversation

For Sherene Woolcock

Your ideas, and what I understood you to say.

Notes from our conversation, organized into a roadmap a family could follow.

Sherene, I took notes while we talked, and afterward I tried to put what you described into an order a family could follow. When you talk about care there's an order in it: understand the person, then work out what good care looks like, then run it and hand it back to the family. Those are the three phases below, with three steps in each. It's your thinking, organized, and I want to know where I've got it wrong.

PHASE 1 · ASSESS

Understand the person, the family, and the situation.

  1. 1
    DiscoverUnderstanding Your Family's Care SituationWrite down where things stand today, what has become hard, and what the family wants to protect.
  2. 2
    AssessUnderstanding Your Loved One's NeedsBuild a clear picture of health, daily function, safety, and the preferences a caregiver should know.
  3. 3
    Define NeedsCreating the Care Needs ProfileTurn what you've learned into the needs, risks, and priorities that point to the right level of care.

PHASE 2 · PLAN

Determine what good care should look like and prepare to put it in place.

  1. 4
    Explore OptionsChoosing the Right Type of CareCompare care settings and providers, and agree on how the family will make the decision.
  2. 5
    Build the PlanBuilding the Personal Care PlanSet down the health and personal care, the daily life worth preserving, and what to watch for.
  3. 6
    Prepare the TransitionPreparing for the TransitionGet ready for a move or a new caregiver so nothing important is lost along the way.

PHASE 3 · MANAGE

Coordinate the plan, review what happens, and prepare the family to take the lead.

  1. 7
    CoordinateCoordinating the Care TeamSettle who does what, how information is shared, and how the family works with the provider's plan.
  2. 8
    MonitorMonitoring and AdvocatingKnow what good care looks like, when to speak up, and how to keep the plan current.
  3. 9
    Hand OffTaking the LeadLearn the skills to manage care yourselves, with support when you need it.

Every step has a version for families who need care now and a version for families planning ahead; a later page explains the difference. The names on the steps are the first thing I'd expect you to change.

What's on the pages that follow

What you told me and what I noticed. Your story, as I'd hope to tell it with your permission. The two kinds of family the roadmap serves. The line between what you do and what you'd never do. Then one question. The appendix holds the course and marketing ideas I drafted for each step: a shared library we can both work from, and one that will keep changing.

Notes byRichard Ladson, Certified Medicaid Planner
ForSherene Woolcock, Senior Care Consultant
What I know about youWhat you told me, and what I noticed

What you told me, and what I noticed.

I'm starting from your words, not from a template.

Your goal

$10,000 a month

On top of what you do now. Not by finding more hours; you don't have them.

Your mission

To serve

Seniors and the families around them. You've held support groups for caregivers. You help people for free because that's who you are.

Your expertise

Memory care

Alzheimer's and dementia. Care plans, managing caregivers, what a good day looks like and what a bad night means. Plus the management experience to run it.

What I noticed

What you have

  • Ideas for a business you've carried for years.
  • Families already coming to you. That's demand, and it's the hardest thing to build.
  • A community you've already built, one support group at a time.
  • Your own story, with your father and your mother.

What's in the way

  • No written process, so every family starts from scratch and you're the only one who can help.
  • No pricing, so the help is free by default, and free doesn't scale or fund itself.
  • The business side, websites and software: work you don't enjoy and shouldn't have to do.

What I took from it

The generosity was never the problem. Without a structure it can reach one family at a time, and a structure is what would let it reach more. That's the thought behind the roadmap on the pages that follow.

Your storyThe reason families will trust you before they read a word

Your story is the front door.

Every family that finds you will want to know one thing before they read a checklist: does she understand what this is like? You do, and not from a textbook.

What I'd tell them, in your words, with your permission

You cared for your father. You've cared for your mother. You've sat in the chair every family caregiver sits in, the one where you're the daughter and the nurse and the scheduler at once, and you've run the support groups where caregivers say out loud what they can't say at home. Then you spent a career learning how care actually gets organized, delivered and managed. There is no one else with both halves of that.

Why I wrote it down

A family chooses a guide they believe has walked the road. Your story does that before you say a word, and the support groups you've hosted are the proof of it. I've put it near the front because, to me, it is the front.

The rule

Nothing about your family appears anywhere until you've written it yourself and said yes. This page is a placeholder for your words, not mine.

Two versionsNeed care now · Plan ahead

Two Versions of Every Step

Most families are deciding in a crisis; some have time to plan. So every step is drawn twice: once for the family in the middle of it, once for the family ahead of it. Not softer wording: different work, different completion.

Need Care Now

Care decisions, a transition, care-delivery concerns, or caregiver overload need attention now.

Understand the needs. Organize the plan. Coordinate the care.

Sherene helps families whose loved one needs care now understand the situation, organize a person-centered plan, and coordinate what happens next—without having to start every conversation from scratch, carry every task alone, or enter care meetings unprepared, even if the family is overwhelmed or unsure where to begin.

Plan Ahead

The family has time to document preferences, discuss roles, explore options, and prepare for changes.

Start the conversation. Prepare the family. Know when to act.

Sherene helps families prepare for an aging loved one’s changing care needs by documenting what matters, organizing a practical care roadmap, and preparing family roles and handoffs—without waiting for a crisis to start the conversation, assuming one person will handle everything, or making a placement decision before it is needed, even if their loved one is still largely independent.

The lineWhat you do · what you never do

Where the Line Is

The framework organizes care information and prepares the family. It does not replace a clinician's plan, and it does not touch money. The left side is my read of the work you described. The right side we didn't really get to, so those are questions, not notes.

What you do

  • Care discovery, and assessment within your confirmed scope.
  • Care-plan preparation and provider-comparison support.
  • Transition coordination and care-plan meetings.
  • Family education, advocacy, and a practiced handoff.
  • Optional support after the handoff.

What you never do

We didn't really talk about this, and it matters for every page that says “within scope.” What I'd like to ask:

  • Where does your work stop and a doctor's or nurse's begin? Medications, diagnoses, when a symptom needs a clinician.
  • When a family asks about paying for care, or about Medi-Cal, what do you do today?
  • When the family's wishes and the person's own wishes differ, whose do you follow?
  • What would you never promise a family, however much they wanted to hear it?
  • Is there anything families ask you for that you always refer out?
One questionDid I hear you right?

Did I hear you right?

That's the whole ask. Read it and tell me what's wrong, what's missing, and what you'd never say to a family.

What would help most

  • The names on the nine steps, and their order. Change anything.
  • What you're licensed or trained to assess, so every page that says “within scope” is true.
  • Anything I put in your mouth that you didn't say.

What happens next

Nothing, until you've reacted. If the roadmap holds up, there's more I'd like to show you about how I'd build around it, but that's a later conversation, and when to have it is your call.

The appendix

The pages after this one are course ideas and marketing ideas for each step, in both versions. They will change and evolve, but they show how I plan to market and sell the courses, and how I think about education and marketing. Use them however you wish. Think of them as a library we share, a single source of truth so we're on the same page, and expect it to change regularly.

AppendixEverything in the package, one page each

They will change and evolve over time, but this is how I plan to market and sell the courses, and I'm sharing them so you can see how I think about both education and marketing. Appendix A · BoundariesFrom the package

Boundaries

Service scopeSherene’s working lane is care discovery, assessment within confirmed scope, planning support, coordination, family education, advocacy, and handoff. Funding, Medicaid eligibility, insurance-funding, and asset planning are excluded.
Professional rolesThe curriculum organizes care information and prepares questions. It does not authorize families or AI to diagnose, prescribe, change medication, set clinical thresholds, or replace a provider’s clinical plan.
Person-centered careThe loved one’s stated preferences remain separate from family wishes. Activity support should preserve choice rather than require attendance.
Draft versus deliveryCourse completion produces an organized learner output. It is not proof of safe placement, a guaranteed care result, or confirmation that Sherene has accepted a professional engagement.
Unknowns and evidenceProvider availability, capabilities, information access, and the actual care-plan review schedule require case-specific confirmation. Missing evidence is not an on-plan status.
Unconfirmed business detailsSherene’s credentials, included meetings, service area, support cadence, response expectations, and directory/data access remain to be confirmed. No prices or financial projections are included.
Advertising statusAds are draft copy. No assertion is made about current ad-platform eligibility, approved targeting, conversion rates, or a live landing page. Claims and destinations need review before launch.
Appendix B · Service tiersFrom the package

Service tiers

High-touch: Sherene leads the coordinationPersonal family discovery and assessment within scope; care-plan preparation; provider-comparison support; transition coordination; explicitly included care-plan meetings; a practiced family handoff. Number of meetings and ongoing monitoring are not assumed.
Guided: Sherene teaches and reviewsThe family uses the same templates and courses with defined group coaching, office hours, or review support. Individual clinical questions are routed to the appropriate professional rather than answered by a generic group curriculum.
Self-directed: the family learns the processCourses, checklists, prompts, worksheets, and planning templates. Community access may be an optional addition. Self-study does not replace a professional assessment or create an ongoing care-management relationship.
Continuity: support after the handoffOptional scheduled check-ins, future meeting help, a moderated community, or periodic gatherings. Scope, cadence, coverage during absence, and response expectations must be agreed; no unlimited access is implied.
Appendix C · MetricsProposed, non-clinical

Proposed non-clinical metrics

MeasureQuestionHow it is recorded
Responsibility coverageWhich active coordination tasks have a confirmed owner and backup?Task table; confirmation date; not a clinical-quality score.
Open follow-upHow many agreed follow-up items are open or past their agreed date?Open, waiting, overdue, resolved; retain the source of the date.
Handoff completionWhich transfers have a recorded recipient acknowledgment?Sent, received, needs clarification, resolved.
Information freshnessWhen was the family plan or contact list last reviewed?Document version and last-reviewed date; no universal review interval assumed.
Caregiver capacityDoes the lead caregiver report that current responsibilities are manageable?A conversation prompt and agreed action, not a diagnostic burnout score.
Person’s experienceWhat does the person report about routines, choices, and meaningful activities?Use their words where possible; record offers and support without rewarding forced participation.
Care-plan follow-throughWhat is known about a small set of agreed care-plan items?Observed, reported, unknown, or needs follow-up, with source and date; clinical interpretation remains with professionals.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Record the event or change that created the immediate need.
  2. Confirm upcoming care decisions and any stated dates.
  3. Name a temporary family contact and a backup.

Working actions

  1. Document where the person lives and who provides help.
  2. Describe morning, daytime, evening, and overnight arrangements.
  3. List family members, professionals, and contact details.
  4. Record what each person actually does.
  5. Ask the primary caregiver which responsibilities are becoming difficult.
  6. Gather relevant existing care notes with appropriate permission.
  7. Separate confirmed facts, family observations, and unanswered questions.
  8. Review the summary with the loved one where possible and with the family.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The family and Sherene have a current summary, an identified contact, and a list of immediate decisions with unknowns clearly marked.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Start with the immediate decision
    • What triggered the request for help.
    • Which decision is next.
    • Who needs the situation summary today.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe the situation
    • Separate current arrangements from proposed changes.
    • Describe a typical day rather than relying on broad labels.
    • Record what changed and when.
  3. Lesson 3 · Map the people and work
    • List family and professional caregivers.
    • Compare actual workload with assumed responsibilities.
    • Identify the person coordinating information.
  4. Lesson 4 · Build the starting summary
    • Combine notes without erasing disagreement.
    • Mark unknown information rather than filling gaps.
    • Prepare a focused review with Sherene.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Something happened with your father, a fall, a hospital stay, a call from a neighbor, and now several people need to understand the situation at once. You have texts, half-remembered phone calls, and a feeling that someone else is handling the important parts.

Where they want to be

You can explain in two minutes what changed, who is involved, and what decision comes next, and you know which pieces are still missing.

Intermediate winI can tell your father's story once, on one page, with the unknowns marked instead of guessed.
Consumer outputA one-page situation brief with four headings: What Happened, Who Is Involved and What They Do, The Decision in Front of Us, and What We Still Need to Find Out.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview walks through your father's living arrangement, his typical day, and every area of daily life in order, checks what has been left out, and produces the Family Care Profile. Sherene's family interview and her reading of the profile follow from there.
Stop lineDo not produce the Family Care Situation Summary, judge whether your father is safe where he is, recommend which option the family should choose, or stand in for the care interview or Sherene's review.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Telling the same story to every new person who asks.
  • Working from notes scattered across texts, voicemails, and memory.
  • Assuming someone else has an important task covered.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Put the last two weeks in order When several things happen fast, the order gets lost, and the order matters. A nurse's comment on Tuesday means something different if the fall was on Monday.
  2. Find out who is actually doing what In a hurry, families assume. Your brother thinks you called the pharmacy. You think he did. Your father's care is whatever the gaps allow.
  3. Name the decision in front of you A crisis blurs together what is happening now, what someone has proposed, and what the family must actually decide. Separating them makes the next conversation shorter.
  4. Write the page you can hand to anyone The discharge planner, your aunt, the doctor's office, and your sister all want the same story. Writing it once saves you from telling it twenty times, and it keeps the story the same each time.

Draft written 2026-10-02 for review.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Begin before decisions become urgent
    • Invite participation rather than announce a decision.
    • Document existing help.
    • Set a sensible reason to review the picture again.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe the situation
    • Separate current arrangements from proposed changes.
    • Describe a typical day rather than relying on broad labels.
    • Record what changed and when.
  3. Lesson 3 · Map the people and work
    • List family and professional caregivers.
    • Compare actual workload with assumed responsibilities.
    • Identify the person coordinating information.
  4. Lesson 4 · Build the starting summary
    • Combine notes without erasing disagreement.
    • Mark unknown information rather than filling gaps.
    • Prepare a focused review with Sherene.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom is doing fine, mostly. Nothing has happened. But you've noticed the small things, a sister who drives her to appointments, a neighbor who brings in the mail, and you suspect the family would not tell the same story if asked.

Where they want to be

You have one shared picture of her week and the help around her, written while everyone is calm, and the family knows where it is kept.

Intermediate winI can describe my mother's ordinary week and the help already in place, and I know what the family still hasn't compared notes on.
Consumer outputA one-page family snapshot with four headings: Her Ordinary Week, Help Already in Place, Where Our Pictures Differ, and Things to Gather While There Is Time.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview covers each part of Mom's daily life in turn, including the areas no one in the family has thought to mention, flags what is incomplete, and builds the Family Care Profile that Sherene reviews with you.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Care Situation Summary, rate how well Mom is managing, suggest that she needs more help or less, or push the family toward any change in where she lives.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Waiting for something to go wrong before the family compares notes.
  • Assuming your brothers and sisters see the same situation you do.
  • Not counting the everyday help that keeps things running.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Let her describe an ordinary week The best source on Mom's week is Mom. Asking her to describe it, rather than announcing that the family is 'getting organized,' keeps her in charge of her own story.
  2. Count the help that is already there Rides, bill paying, a weekly phone call, someone who changes the smoke detector battery. None of it feels like caregiving, and all of it is. Written down, it shows how much is already being done and by whom.
  3. Compare what each relative sees Everyone in the family has a slightly different mother. The sibling who visits on Sundays and the one who calls on Wednesday nights are seeing different hours of the same week. The differences are useful, not a problem.
  4. Make the snapshot and decide when to look again A snapshot is only useful if someone can find it and knows when to update it. The last job is to put everything on one page and name the kinds of changes that would mean it's time to look again.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father's care isn't working and everyone has a theory. Your sister, who does most of it, is exhausted and short with everyone. Phone calls turn into arguments about whose fault it is, and nobody can say exactly what is going wrong.

Where they want to be

You can name the real problems with an example for each, say which tasks are not getting done, state plainly what your sister needs, and know which concerns belong with a professional.

Intermediate winI can list what is actually going wrong with my father's care, with examples instead of accusations, and I can see how close my sister is to the edge.
Consumer outputA one-page concerns list with four headings: What Is Going Wrong (one example each), What Is Not Getting Done, What the Caregiver Needs Now, and Who Should Hear About Each One.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview asks about your father's daily life and the care around him in a set order, so that problems the family hasn't noticed surface alongside the ones that have, and it records them in the Family Care Profile. Sherene brings caregiver strain, family disagreement, and unmet tasks into one conversation and decides what each one calls for.
Stop lineDo not build the Family Care Challenges Register, decide whose fault anything is, judge whether your father is safe, say whether a move is needed, or weigh in on any medication or treatment question.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Trying to settle every disagreement in one phone call.
  • Letting worries come out as accusations.
  • Not noticing that the person doing most of the work is nearly out of capacity.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Turn the complaints into examples 'Nobody is looking after him properly' starts a fight. 'He missed his Tuesday appointment and no one knew until Thursday' starts a conversation. The difference is an example.
  2. Find the tasks that are slipping Care breaks down one task at a time. The prescription that didn't get picked up, the bill that didn't get paid, the shower that keeps getting skipped. A list of tasks and their actual status is more useful than a general sense that things are falling apart.
  3. Hear the caregiver before she stops talking The person doing most of the work is often the last to be asked how she's doing and the first to be criticized. If your sister stops, everything stops. Her answer to 'what can't go on like this' is the most important information in this guide.
  4. Decide who needs to hear what Not everything belongs in the family meeting, and not everything belongs with the doctor. Sorting the concerns by who should hear them stops one conversation from trying to carry everything.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

You look after your husband, and it works, more or less. The kids help when they can. But the list of things you do has grown without anyone deciding it should, and there's a conversation with your daughter you keep not having.

Where they want to be

You can say what has gotten harder, point to the tasks that are nobody's job in particular, and raise one difficult subject with the family while it is still a conversation rather than an emergency.

Intermediate winI can see where the arrangement is wearing thin, and I have one honest page to show the family before anything breaks.
Consumer outputA one-page stress-points sheet with four headings: What Is Getting Harder, Where Nobody Is Sure Who Does It, The Conversation to Have Soon, and What We Will Watch.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview covers your husband's needs and the help around him area by area, including the ones that feel too ordinary to mention, and records the whole arrangement in the Family Care Profile. Sherene looks at the profile with you and the family, including how much is resting on one person, and advises within her professional scope.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Care Challenges Register, judge whether the arrangement is failing, tell the family that more help or a move is needed, or offer advice about your husband's condition or your own health.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Treating a heavy week as just what caregiving is.
  • Expecting the tasks that keep getting missed to sort themselves out.
  • Putting off the hard conversation until something forces it.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Look at your own week honestly Caregiving grows quietly. A year ago you didn't manage his pills or drive him everywhere, and now you do, and it feels normal because it arrived one task at a time. Writing the week down lets you see its real size.
  2. Find the tasks nobody has quite agreed to In a family arrangement, half the work happens because someone assumed someone else would do it, or because one person stopped waiting. Those tasks are the ones that get missed when a week goes wrong.
  3. Name the conversation you've been putting off Most families have one subject that nobody raises: a son who promised more than he delivers, a disagreement about whether he should still drive, a daughter who thinks everything is fine. The longer it waits, the harder it gets, and the more likely it is to come out badly.
  4. Put the stress points on one page One honest page, written while things are still working, is worth more than a long conversation after they stop. It also makes it acceptable to ask for help, because the asking is already on paper.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

A care decision has to be made soon for the person you're caring for, and the family does not agree. One relative has strong opinions and a loud voice. Somewhere in the hurry, what the person themselves wants has started to go quiet.

Where they want to be

You can say in their words what the person wants, show where the family agrees and where it doesn't, and list the questions that have to be answered before anyone decides.

Intermediate winI can put the person's own wishes next to each relative's view, without pretending we all agree, and I know what we still need to find out before we decide.
Consumer outputA one-page meeting sheet with four headings: What They Have Told Us They Want, Where We Agree, Where We Don't, and Questions to Answer Before We Decide.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview records the person's situation across every area of daily life, so the family's priorities sit next to a complete picture of what the decision is actually about, and builds the Family Care Profile. Sherene asks the person what is important to them, helps the family see agreement and disagreement clearly, and works out with you what the family can realistically contribute.
Stop lineDo not create the What Matters Most Profile, settle the disagreement, write the family's decision criteria for them, recommend an option, compare specific places or services, or decide whether the person is safe.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming the whole family wants the same outcome.
  • Letting whoever talks most decide the plan.
  • Losing the person's own preferences in the rush to decide.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Start with what they have actually said Under pressure, families begin speaking for the person. 'She'd never want that' and 'He'll be fine with it' are guesses dressed as facts. Their own words, even a few of them, carry more weight than any relative's summary.
  2. Give every relative the same three questions Disagreement is easier to see when everyone answers the same questions in the same shape. It also stops one person's long argument from counting more than another's short one.
  3. Name the decision and what it depends on 'What should we do about Dad' is not a decision. 'Does she go home from rehab on the 14th or somewhere else first' is. A named decision shows you what facts it rests on, and which of those facts you don't have.
  4. Write the sheet for the family meeting A meeting with a sheet in front of it stays on the subject. A meeting without one is decided by whoever is most tired of talking. The sheet keeps the person's words at the top of the page and the disagreements in plain view.

Three priority actions

Working actions

  1. Ask the loved one what matters most to them.
  2. Record routines and choices they want preserved.
  3. Ask each involved family member about concerns and desired outcomes.
  4. Separate the person’s wishes from the family’s preferences.
  5. Document where expectations conflict.
  6. Discuss what relatives can and cannot realistically provide.
  7. List questions requiring clinical or other professional clarification.
  8. Agree on criteria to use when comparing care options.

    • Ask what makes a good day.
    • Capture their own words when possible.
    • Do not replace their preferences with family assumptions.
  3. Lesson 3 · Listen to the family
    • Explore hopes and worries.
    • Separate preferences from available caregiving capacity.
    • Identify competing expectations.

    • Record agreement and disagreement.
    • Identify tradeoffs for discussion.
    • Keep unresolved issues visible in the planning file.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife is well and independent, and the subject of future care has never come up. You'd like to know what she would want preserved if things change, and you don't want the first conversation to sound like a plan to move her anywhere.

Where they want to be

You've had a first conversation that stayed about her life, not about a move. You know what she wants to keep, and the family has said honestly what each person could offer.

Intermediate winI can say what my wife wants preserved, in her words, and what the rest of us can realistically promise, with the hard questions saved rather than skipped.
Consumer outputA one-page starting point with four headings: What She Wants to Keep, How We Raised It and What She Said, What Each of Us Can Honestly Offer, and Questions for Later.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview records your wife's situation across every area of daily life, so her wishes sit alongside a complete account of how she lives now, and keeps it in a Family Care Profile the family can update as things change. Sherene asks her directly what is important to her and helps the family understand what it can realistically contribute.
Stop lineDo not create the What Matters Most Profile, propose a move or a service, draft decision criteria, judge whether your wife needs support, or let the conversation turn into a plan for anything she hasn't asked to plan.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Waiting until a choice has to be made in a hurry.
  • Assuming that because she's independent, there's nothing to talk about.
  • Promising care that relatives won't realistically be able to give.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Find a gentle way in The hardest part is the first sentence. If it sounds like a plan, she'll hear a verdict. If it starts with permission and with ordinary life, it's just a conversation between two people who've had thousands.
  2. Write down what she wants to keep Once she's talked, the risk is that you remember what you expected to hear. Writing her words down soon after, and separating them from your own conclusions, protects what she actually said.
  3. Be honest about what each of you can offer In a calm moment, it's easy to say 'we'll take care of you.' Later, a son with a job two states away can't, and the promise becomes a wound. Asking what each person could really do, and what would change it, is kinder than any promise.
  4. Make the page you'll come back to This isn't a plan. It's a starting point, written while there is time, that the family can read again in a year and change. The last job is to put it on one page and keep the unanswered questions visible instead of letting them disappear.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom came home from the hospital and “needs more help.” Nobody has said what that means, and you're filling the gaps from the diagnosis.

Where they want to be

You can describe what she can do, where she already gets help, and the questions a professional still has to answer.

Intermediate winI can describe what I've actually observed, where Mom already gets help, and what I still don't know.
Consumer outputA one-page list: What we know, What we don't know, Questions we need answered, and who to ask.
Reserved for the softwareThe structured care interview across every care domain, the completeness check, the observations, and the Family Care Profile itself (family copy and professional copy).
Stop lineDo not determine care needs, conduct the complete interview, or create the Personal Care Assessment Summary or Family Care Profile.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Guessing from the diagnosis alone.
  • Overlooking the help already being provided.
  • Mistaking a family worksheet for a clinical assessment.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Start with what you've actually seen It's easy to think about the diagnosis instead of what happens at breakfast, in the bathroom, or getting to the car. The diagnosis is important, but it doesn't tell you what Mom did this morning.
  2. Count the help that's already happening Families underestimate the care they already provide. One person handles pills, someone brings groceries, a neighbor checks in. Mom may be "independent" because five people quietly make it so.
  3. Find out what you don't know yet The most useful thing the AI can do here is not answer questions. It's to show you the questions you haven't asked.
  4. Sort your questions by who can answer them Some questions you can answer by paying attention. Others need a nurse, a doctor, a pharmacist, or a care consultant. Knowing which is which is the whole point of this guide.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Dad still lives in his own place and handles most things himself. Nothing has gone wrong. You've just started to wonder whether some things take him longer than they used to, and you realize you have no record to compare against.

Where they want to be

You have a dated snapshot of what Dad does on his own and where the family already steps in, plus a short list of changes that would be worth raising with his doctor.

Intermediate winI can describe what an ordinary week looks like for Dad right now, in writing, with a date on it.
Consumer outputA one-page baseline: What Dad does on his own, Where the family already helps, What we've noticed changing, and What would prompt a conversation with a professional.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview asks about every area of daily life in order, catches what the family skipped, records each observation with its source and date, and produces the Family Care Profile that Sherene reviews. The guide gives you a rough baseline; the interview gives you a complete one.
Stop lineDo not predict decline, interpret an observation as a symptom, decide when reassessment is due, or produce the Personal Care Baseline and Preferences Profile or the Personal Care Assessment Summary.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Relying on memory to compare changes.
  • Overlooking the gradual increase in family help.
  • Drawing clinical conclusions from isolated observations.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Describe an ordinary week You'll compare against this later. A week recorded now, with a date on it, beats trying to remember next year how things used to be.
  2. Notice how much the family already does Help grows a little at a time. Someone started driving him to appointments two years ago. Someone else quietly took over the bills. Nobody counts it, so nobody notices it has doubled.
  3. Separate what you saw from what you concluded One forgotten appointment is a fact. “His memory is going” is a conclusion. Writing both down as if they were the same thing makes the baseline less useful and the worry bigger.
  4. Agree on what would prompt a conversation Planning ahead doesn't mean watching for everything. It means knowing which changes matter enough to call someone, so the rest of the time you can relax.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your husband is being discharged, or moving to a new arrangement, within days. Everyone says they'll pitch in. You have a feeling the plan rests on you being awake at 3 a.m. and on a daughter who lives two hours away.

Where they want to be

You can show, on one page, when he will need someone, who has actually said yes, where the gaps are, and which concerns you are taking to the care team rather than settling yourself.

Intermediate winI can see the hours nobody has covered, and I know which questions aren't mine to answer.
Consumer outputA one-page coverage review: When help is needed, Who has committed, Gaps and backup, Concerns for the care team, and Who follows up on each.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview asks systematically about falls, supervision, medication handling, the home environment, and each caregiver's limits, checks the coverage you describe against the needs you describe, and records it all in the Family Care Profile. Sherene reviews the profile and tells you which gaps matter, within her scope.
Stop lineDo not declare the arrangement safe or unsafe, decide whether he should come home, write care instructions, settle a medication concern, or produce the Safety and Support Review.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming help will be available because people said so.
  • Overlooking overnight coverage.
  • Asking one caregiver to carry more than they can sustain.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Lay out when help will be needed A list of what he needs isn't the same as a clock. Getting up at night, the first hour of the morning, and meals are when help is needed most, and they are the hardest hours to fill.
  2. Check who is really available “I'll help” and “I can be there Tuesdays and Thursdays from 9 to 2” are different things. The first is kindness. The second is coverage.
  3. Be honest about what you can carry The plan usually assumes the main caregiver can do whatever is left over. If that's you, your limits are part of the safety picture, not a weakness in it.
  4. Sort the gaps you can fill from the ones a professional must see Some gaps are solved by a phone call to a cousin. Others, like a fall risk or a medication he can't manage alone, are not yours to settle. The care team needs to hear those before the move, not after.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your mother is doing fine at home, and the help around her has settled into a routine that works. Nobody has fallen, nothing has broken. You just haven't asked what happens if your brother takes that job out of state, or if the neighbor who checks in moves away.

Where they want to be

You can describe how your mother's week is held together, which pieces depend on one person, who could step in, and which small concerns you would rather raise now than later.

Intermediate winI can name the people my mother's routine depends on, and I know which of them have no backup.
Consumer outputA one-page support map: Who helps and when, What we're assuming, Backup for each role, and Concerns worth raising now.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview walks through supervision, falls, medication handling, the home environment, and each caregiver's capacity in a set order, so the family's map is checked against the full set of questions rather than the ones that came to mind. The result is recorded in the Family Care Profile, which Sherene reviews within her scope.
Stop lineDo not assess the home, judge whether the current arrangement is adequate, assign anyone a caregiving role, recommend a service, or create the Safety and Support Review.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Waiting until the coverage fails before looking at it.
  • Assuming family availability will stay the way it is.
  • Overlooking the need for a backup caregiver.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Map an ordinary week of help Routines become invisible. The help your mother gets probably works so smoothly that nobody has written it down, which is exactly why nobody can see where it's thin.
  2. Find the assumptions holding it together Every arrangement rests on a few quiet assumptions: that your sister stays nearby, that the neighbor keeps checking in, that your mother keeps driving. Naming them isn't pessimism. It's the planning part of planning ahead.
  3. Name a backup for each role A backup doesn't have to be another relative. It can be a friend, a service you have looked into, or simply knowing who you would call. What matters is that the answer exists before you need it.
  4. Set aside the concerns worth raising now Small things you've noticed, a wobble on the stairs, pills in the wrong day of the box, a stove left on once, are easier to mention to a professional when nothing is urgent. Writing them down keeps them from being forgotten or inflated.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife is moving into a new care setting this week, or new caregivers are about to start coming to the house. You know she takes her tea before anything else and can't stand being called “sweetie.” They don't, and you can't be there every hour to tell them.

Where they want to be

You can hand the new team a page that tells them who she is and what makes a day go well for her, with her wishes and her medical instructions kept clearly apart.

Intermediate winI can put the things that matter most to my wife on one page a stranger could read in two minutes.
Consumer outputA one-page About Me draft: How to address me, My mornings and evenings, Food I like and food I'm told to avoid, What I enjoy and who matters to me, How to talk with me, and What helps when I'm unsettled.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview asks about preferences across every part of the day alongside her care needs and support, flags where the family's account and her own may differ, and keeps the About Me material inside the Family Care Profile with its source and date. Sherene reviews the profile and helps the family decide what to share and with whom.
Stop lineDo not write care instructions, convert a preference into a dietary or medical order, decide what she would want if she cannot say, name a facility or agency, or produce the finished About Me Care Profile.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Relying on relatives to repeat every detail to every new caregiver.
  • Losing familiar routines in the rush of an admission.
  • Writing down what the family wants instead of what she wants.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Start with her own account of a good day The fastest way to end up with your version of her preferences is to skip asking her. Even a short conversation, even one with gaps, puts her voice at the center of the page.
  2. Pull out what the new caregivers need on day one A new caregiver has about two minutes for your page. The small things that keep her steady in a strange place, when she wakes, what she drinks first, which side of the bed, are the ones that get lost in a move.
  3. Keep her preferences separate from her care orders “She doesn't like fish” and “she has a nut allergy” are both about food, but one is a preference and the other is an instruction from a clinician. If they sit in the same list, staff may treat both as optional or both as orders.
  4. Draft the About Me page Now you have her words, the day-one details, and the preferences kept apart from the orders. The last step is making it short enough that it actually gets read.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father is well and nobody is talking about caregivers. But you've noticed how much you would have to guess if someone else ever had to look after him for a week, and you would rather ask him now, over coffee, than find out later that nobody wrote down how he likes his eggs.

Where they want to be

You have a first version of your father's preferences in his own words, you know which of your assumptions he corrected, and the page has a date and a plan to update it.

Intermediate winI can say what makes an ordinary day good for my father because I asked him, not because I assumed.
Consumer outputA one-page preferences draft: How I like to be addressed, My ordinary day, Food and routines I enjoy, People and activities that matter to me, How I like to be spoken to, and When to ask me again.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview collects preferences alongside his abilities, health information, and support in one structured pass, notes where his account and the family's differ, and stores it in the Family Care Profile with a source and date so it can be updated. Sherene reviews the profile and helps the family think about when and with whom it should be shared.
Stop lineDo not decide what he would want in a situation he hasn't discussed, write dietary or care instructions, treat today's answers as permanent, or produce the finished About Me Care Profile.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming the relatives already know all the details.
  • Waiting for a crisis before asking personal questions.
  • Treating preferences from years ago as if they can't change.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Turn a conversation into questions worth asking You're not interviewing him. You're having a conversation that happens to leave notes behind. A handful of open questions makes that easier than a checklist ever will.
  2. Learn what makes an ordinary day good The details that matter in care are usually small: the radio station, the second cup of coffee, the walk after lunch. He may not think they are worth mentioning. Your notes will show you they are.
  3. Check what you assumed against what he said Families carry old facts around. He hated church as a young man; he goes every week now. He always drank tea; he switched to coffee a decade ago. The point isn't to catch anyone out. It's to find out which of your facts are current.
  4. Start a preferences page built to be revised This isn't a final document. It's a first draft with a date on it, written so it is easy to change. That's what keeps it honest a year from now.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father has a care plan on paper, an agency on the calendar, and a sister who covers everything in between. Something isn't getting done, and you can't tell yet whether it's the service, the schedule, or just that nobody has checked.

Where they want to be

You can say which of your father's needs are reliably covered, which ones you have only assumed are covered, and who you need to call to find out.

Intermediate winI can see the difference between the help your father is supposed to get and the help he actually gets, and I know what still needs checking.
Consumer outputA one-page list with three headings: Covered and Confirmed, Not Sure Yet, and Nobody Is Covering This, with a name to call next to each item under Not Sure Yet.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview takes your father's situation area by area and records the support in place for each need, so the gaps are found against a complete picture rather than your memory. The course builds the Care Needs and Gaps Register with sources, owners, and status for every gap. Sherene reads the gaps alongside her own observations and decides which ones need clinical review.
Stop lineDo not build the Care Needs and Gaps Register, declare that a service has failed, judge whether your father is safe, or recommend changing his care or any provider.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming a service that's on the schedule is actually being delivered.
  • Treating something you haven't confirmed as if it has already failed.
  • Missing the gaps one worn-out relative is quietly filling.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Line up what's needed against what's scheduled A care plan tells you what was arranged. It doesn't tell you what happened on Tuesday. Most families read the schedule and assume the visit took place.
  2. Separate what's unconfirmed from what's broken When you're worried, an unanswered question feels like proof. Most of what looks like a failure is really something nobody has checked yet, and the two call for very different phone calls.
  3. Count the help that isn't on any schedule The gaps that hurt most are often invisible because one relative fills them without being asked. Her effort hides the gap until the day she can't do it.
  4. Put it on one page Three lists are easier to act on than a stack of notes. The page you make here is what you'll bring to the next conversation with your father's care team, and it stops you from carrying it all in your head.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom is doing well at home. A neighbor drives her to appointments, your brother handles the bills, and you call every evening. It works, and nobody has asked what happens if one piece stops.

Where they want to be

You can name the tasks that rest on a single person, say which backup arrangements are real and which are hopes, and describe the changes that would mean it's time to look again.

Intermediate winI can point to every part of my mother's support that depends on one person, and I know which backups are real.
Consumer outputA one-page map with four headings: Who Does What, Depends on One Person, Backup Confirmed or Not, and Changes That Mean We Should Look Again.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview walks through every area of Mom's life, including the ones that are fine today, so dependencies are found against the full picture rather than the parts you happened to think of. The course turns the map into a Care Needs and Gaps Register that separates present gaps from future contingencies. Sherene reviews the register with her own observations and advises on what to monitor.
Stop lineDo not create the Care Needs and Gaps Register, predict when Mom's needs will change, or recommend adding a service or moving her.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming the help in place today will always be there.
  • Counting a backup plan nobody has actually agreed to as real coverage.
  • Putting off writing down the small needs that aren't met yet.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Map who does what A working arrangement hides its own structure. You know the neighbor drives, but you may not have noticed that nobody else can, or that the evening phone call is the only daily check anyone makes.
  2. Test the backup plans Families say “well, if that happened, Aunt Carol would step in.” Aunt Carol may not know this. A backup that hasn't been agreed to is a wish, and wishes don't drive anyone to the doctor.
  3. Write down the small gaps now Nothing has gone wrong, which is exactly why the small unmet needs get ignored. Written down today, they're a note. Discovered during a crisis, they're one more emergency.
  4. Name the changes worth watching, and put it on one page A map of today is only useful if you know when to redraw it. The changes that matter are usually ordinary and noticeable: a helper moves, a stair gets harder, a bill goes unpaid.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

The hospital social worker has started saying “assisted living” and “memory care,” and a decision about your wife is a few weeks away at most. You know what she needs at home, hour by hour. You don't know what those labels actually cover.

Where they want to be

You can describe the help your wife needs in plain tasks, separate what any arrangement must provide from what you'd simply like, and hand her care team a list of what they need to confirm before you choose.

Intermediate winI can say, in plain words, what help my wife needs every day and which questions a professional has to settle before we pick anything.
Consumer outputA one-page list with three headings: Help She Needs Every Day, Must Have Versus Would Like, and Questions for Her Care Team.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview records your wife's needs in every area of daily life, including the ones that don't show up at home, and produces the Family Care Profile that any discussion of settings should start from. The course turns the profile into a Care Requirements Brief with confirmed frequencies and the capabilities providers must be asked to verify. Sherene translates assessed needs into the amount and type of assistance required and flags what needs clinical confirmation.
Stop lineDo not write the Care Requirements Brief, say which level of care your wife needs, match her to a type of setting or a named provider, or state how often she needs help unless you observed it yourself.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Picking a setting from its name instead of from what she needs.
  • Assuming every place with the same label provides the same help.
  • Settling her care needs yourselves when a professional should weigh in.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Describe the help in tasks, not labels “Assisted living” and “memory care” are categories, not descriptions of your wife. What you can describe is who helps her stand up, who reminds her to eat, and when. That's the language a decision should be made in.
  2. Sort must-haves from would-likes Two places with the same sign on the door can offer very different help. You can only tell them apart if you know which of your wife's needs are non-negotiable and which are preferences.
  3. Find the questions only her care team can answer Some of what your wife needs is for a clinician to settle, not for you to guess at. Knowing which questions those are, and who answers each, keeps you from deciding her care level over the kitchen table.
  4. Make the page you'll read to the social worker When the social worker calls, you'll want one page, not a folder. This page is what you read from, and what you hand to anyone who wants to help.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father manages at home with a little help, and nothing has gone wrong. Relatives have opinions about where this is heading. You'd rather have a clear record of what he needs now than an argument about what he'll need in five years.

Where they want to be

You can state what support your father requires today, name the specific changes that should send you back to a professional, and list the questions you'd ask when that happens.

Intermediate winI have today's needs written down plainly and I know which changes would mean it's time to ask for new advice.
Consumer outputA one-page record with three headings: Help He Gets Today, Changes Worth a Conversation, and Questions We'd Ask Then.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview records your father's support in every area of life, so the baseline is complete and consistent rather than assembled from memory. The course turns that baseline into a Care Requirements Brief with a professional-review route and agreed reassessment triggers. Sherene decides which changes call for clinical confirmation and what a reassessment should look at.
Stop lineDo not create the Care Requirements Brief, forecast a sequence of care settings for your father, say when he will need more help, or recommend a setting or provider.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Treating care as a fixed sequence of stages he's bound to follow.
  • Assuming the help at home will carry on exactly as it is.
  • Waiting until there's a problem to find out which capabilities matter.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Write down today's help Families skip this because nothing is wrong. But a record of what your father needs now is the only thing that will let you recognize a change later, instead of arguing about whether one happened.
  2. See what the home arrangement is counting on Help at home usually rests on things nobody has said out loud: he still drives, the neighbor is home during the day, the stairs are fine. Each one is an assumption, and assumptions change without warning.
  3. Name the changes worth a conversation You can't predict how your father's needs will change, and you shouldn't try. What you can do is agree now on which changes would make you pick up the phone, and whose number you'd dial.
  4. Date it and keep it to one page A record, a watch list, and a set of questions fit on one page. That page is what you'll pull out when a change happens, so you start from facts instead of from fear.

Reserved for the softwareThe care interview captures your husband's whole situation in the Family Care Profile, which is what the sequence of decisions is built on. The course builds the Family Care Action Roadmap with owners, backups, dates, and completion evidence, and checks whether the lead caregiver's load is realistic. Sherene turns her assessment into the order of care decisions and names which professionals need to be involved.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Care Action Roadmap, assign tasks to people who haven't agreed, decide the care arrangement itself, or set medical or legal deadlines you haven't been given.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Trying to settle everything in the same week.
  • Making a move before the thing it depends on is settled.
  • Letting one person become the coordinator of every task.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Dump everything and sort it When it all feels urgent, the first relief is seeing that half the pile is chores and a third is questions. Only a few items are decisions, and those are the ones that need you.
  2. Find the one decision that's really next Urgency comes from a date. Most of the dates in your head were never given to you by anyone; they're guesses the family has started treating as deadlines.
  3. List what has to be settled first Acting before the groundwork is done is how families end up redoing things. The next decision depends on a few facts, and some of them belong to a doctor, a pharmacist, or a social worker, not to you.
  4. See who's carrying the load, then put it on one page If your name is next to most of the tasks, the plan won't survive the first bad week. This page makes the load visible and gives you a list to hand out.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom is fine, and you'd like to keep it that way without a scramble later. Someone in the family wants to tour places now. Someone else doesn't want to talk about it at all. You want a plan that gets things ready without forcing anything.

Where they want to be

You can say which preparation is worth doing this season, which decisions you're deliberately not making yet, which pieces you'll ask others to take, and what change would bring the family back to the plan.

Intermediate winI can tell useful preparation apart from decisions that aren't due, and I know what would bring us back to the plan.
Consumer outputA one-page plan with four headings: Worth Doing Now, Deliberately Waiting, Preparation to Share, and What Would Wake This Plan Up.
Reserved for the softwareThe care interview records Mom's current situation as a Family Care Profile, the baseline a future roadmap is measured against. The course builds the Family Care Action Roadmap with owners, backups, review dates, and activation triggers, and agrees who maintains the planning file. Sherene reviews the sequence, identifies which professionals should be involved and when, and advises on triggers that reflect her assessment.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Care Action Roadmap, choose or rank places for Mom to live, set a timeline for a move, or assign tasks to relatives who haven't agreed.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Deciding where Mom will live before anything requires it.
  • Letting the whole preparation fall to one person.
  • Writing a plan nobody has a reason to open again.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Sort now from not yet The relative who wants to tour places and the one who won't discuss it are both reacting to the same thing: no one has separated preparation from decisions. Gathering papers is preparation. Choosing a building is a decision, and it isn't due.
  2. Break the preparation into pieces others can take Preparation lands on one person because it looks like one big job. Broken into afternoons, most of it can be done by a sibling three states away.
  3. Name the changes that would wake the plan up A plan with no trigger is a plan nobody reopens. The triggers that work are things you'd notice anyway: a fall, a helper moving away, Mom saying she's lonely.
  4. Put the plan on one page One page the family has seen is worth more than a folder one person keeps. This is the page you'll open when a trigger happens, and the one you'll check against on the date you choose.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Dad can't manage the way he was, and the family is already saying words like “assisted living” and “home care” as if they were answers. You're being asked to decide between names before anyone has written down what the care actually has to do.

Where they want to be

You can say what any arrangement for Dad has to provide, what staying home would require of the family, and what you'd need a provider or a professional to confirm before going further.

Intermediate winI can describe Dad's care in terms of what has to happen each day, not in terms of a type of place.
Consumer outputA one-page sheet: What the care has to cover, What matters to Dad, What home would take, and Questions a provider or professional must answer.
Reserved for the softwareThe Care Settings Comparison Worksheet, the lesson on comparing arrangements against requirements, and the narrowing to options worth investigating belong to the course. Weighing home care, assisted living, memory care, skilled nursing or a continuing-care setting against Dad's actual needs is Sherene's professional work, with the Family Care Profile as her starting file.
Stop lineDo not pick or rule out a care setting, say whether Dad can stay home safely, describe what a particular facility or agency offers, or fill in the Care Settings Comparison Worksheet.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Choosing a setting because the label sounds familiar.
  • Underestimating the support staying home would need.
  • Assuming the setting you pick now can handle whatever comes next.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Translate the needs into plain requirements Settings get chosen by name because the name is easy to say. The hard part is writing down what the care has to do, hour by hour, and that is what every setting must be measured against.
  2. Add up what staying home would take Home is the familiar option, so families often skip the arithmetic. Someone has to do each task on the list, at the hour it's needed, and that someone has a job, a drive, or their own health to think about.
  3. Ask what happens when things change The arrangement that fits today may not fit in six months. The question to ask about any setting, including home, is how it handles more care, and families rarely ask it until they need to.
  4. Put it on one page for the people who can confirm it You now have requirements, the shape of home, and the questions about change. The last job is to put them where a provider, a doctor, or Sherene can see what you need confirmed.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your mother is doing fine. You've watched friends scramble when a parent's situation changed, and you'd rather understand the landscape now than learn it in a hospital hallway. Nobody is moving anywhere.

Where they want to be

You can name the kinds of arrangements your family wants to understand, say what your mother has told you she wants, and describe what would need to be true before any of it became a real question.

Intermediate winI can talk about care options calmly, with my mother's wishes in front of me, and without pretending we're choosing.
Consumer outputA one-page Future Options Notes sheet: What my mother wants, What we know and want to learn about each kind of arrangement, What we'd have to confirm later, and What would bring us back to this.
Reserved for the softwareThe Care Settings Comparison Worksheet, the lesson on separating education from selection, and the preliminary comparison with its revisit points belong to the course. Explaining how home care, assisted living, memory care, skilled nursing and continuing-care settings tend to work, and which of them are worth your mother's family learning more about, is Sherene's professional work.
Stop lineDo not predict your mother's future needs, compare settings or recommend one, describe any particular community or agency, or produce the Care Settings Comparison Worksheet.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Leaving the learning until a decision is forced.
  • Assuming the place she prefers today will always be able to meet her needs.
  • Settling on a setting before anyone knows what the requirements would be.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Write down what your mother has actually said Families carry strong beliefs about what a parent wants, often from one conversation years ago. Before learning about options, it helps to separate what she has said from what you've assumed.
  2. Sort what you think you know about the kinds of care Most of what we know about assisted living, home care, or a nursing home comes from a friend's experience or a commercial. Some of it is right. Writing it down shows where your picture is thin.
  3. Mark what could only be confirmed later Anything you learn now about availability, cost, or what a setting can handle will be out of date by the time it matters. Knowing which facts expire keeps you from building a plan on them.
  4. Write the page you'll come back to This isn't a decision, so the page shouldn't look like one. It should hold your mother's wishes, what you've learned, what's still open, and the signals that would tell you to come back and look harder.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your husband needs more care than you can give at home, or the hospital has told you he'll be discharged somewhere else. You've been handed a list of names, friends have opinions, and a directory says who has beds. None of it is confirmed.

Where they want to be

You can call any agency or facility with the same set of questions, write down the answer, its source, and the date, and know which claims still need checking before you'd trust them.

Intermediate winI know what I need a provider to confirm for my husband, and I'll ask it the same way every time.
Consumer outputA one-page Provider Call Sheet: Our must-haves, Questions we ask every provider, and a blank record with source, date, answer, and still to confirm.
Reserved for the softwareThe Provider Research and Verification Sheet, the search criteria lesson, and the method for separating provider statements from independent quality information belong to the course. Deciding which providers can actually address your husband's documented requirements and which deserve a tour is Sherene's professional work.
Stop lineDo not compare, rank, or recommend providers or facilities, treat any listing as a current bed or shift, judge a provider's quality, or complete the Provider Research and Verification Sheet.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Reading a directory listing as if it were today's availability.
  • Assuming the staff you meet at ten in the morning are the staff on duty at two at night.
  • Deciding on the strength of a brochure, a tour's first impression, or a friend's opinion.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Turn the requirements into must-haves A provider can only be measured against what your husband needs, and a search without must-haves ends up driven by whoever returns the call first.
  2. Separate what you've been told from what you've confirmed By now you've collected names, a brochure, a directory printout, and a cousin's recommendation. All of it feels like information. Only some of it has been checked.
  3. Prepare the questions every provider gets Asking the same questions of everyone is what makes answers comparable later. It also keeps you from forgetting the night shift, the shared room, or what happens when his needs go up.
  4. Build the call sheet The sheet isn't a judgment about anyone. It's a place to write down what each provider says, where it came from, and what's still open, so the comparison can happen later with Sherene.

    • Record the source and date.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Dad is managing well. A neighbor swears by one agency, your aunt has a facility in mind, and you have a vague sense you should be writing something down. There's no deadline, and that's the advantage.

Where they want to be

You can say what your family would need from a provider, which questions turn a name into useful research, and which details will have to be checked again before anyone chooses.

Intermediate winI know what makes a provider name worth keeping, and what about it will need rechecking later.
Consumer outputA one-page Research File Starter: What would matter to our family, Questions to ask any provider, What we'll recheck before choosing, and a blank entry card with source and date.
Reserved for the softwareThe Provider Research and Verification Sheet, the lesson on preserving sources and dates, and the re-verification process belong to the course. Judging which providers are worth Dad's family keeping on file, and reading quality information against his needs, is Sherene's professional work.
Stop lineDo not research, compare, rank or recommend any provider or facility, claim anything about current availability, estimate prices, or produce the Provider Research and Verification Sheet.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Keeping a list of names with nothing beside them that would help you compare.
  • Treating a bed or a schedule that's open today as if it will be open in two years.
  • Taking one person's recommendation without asking the questions Dad's needs would raise.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Decide what would matter to your family Without a short list of what matters, research turns into collecting. Location, family access, and Dad's stated preferences are a good start, even before his needs are known.
  2. See what a recommended name actually tells you A friend's warm recommendation is a reason to ask questions, not a conclusion. Writing down what you actually know about a name usually reveals that you know almost nothing that would help you compare.
  3. Learn the questions that make research useful The difference between a name and a research entry is a set of needs-based questions with dated answers. Knowing the questions now means you won't be learning them under pressure later.
  4. Start the file A good file is mostly structure: what matters, what to ask, what to recheck, and a card per provider with source and date. The names can wait.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife has to move to a new care arrangement soon, and you've toured or called a few places. One felt right. Your daughter prefers another. Everyone has an opinion, and nobody has written down what you're actually comparing against.

Where they want to be

You can walk into the family conversation with the same criteria for every option, a clear list of what's confirmed and what isn't, and the questions still to put to a provider or a professional before anyone signs anything.

Intermediate winI can explain what we're comparing, what we still don't know, and who needs to be in the room, before anyone argues about names.
Consumer outputA one-page Decision Prep Sheet: Our criteria, What we've confirmed, What's still open, Who needs to be in the conversation, and Questions for the next tour or call.
Reserved for the softwareThe Care Option Decision Record, the lesson on comparing options against the same criteria, and the method for documenting disagreement and the decision belong to the course. Comparing the actual options against your wife's needs, helping the family work through disagreement, and interpreting what the providers said is Sherene's professional work.
Stop lineDo not compare, score, rank or recommend the options, declare one safe or unsafe, say who holds legal authority to decide, resolve the family disagreement, or complete the Care Option Decision Record.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Letting the option that felt best on the day carry the decision.
  • Arguing about places before agreeing what you're measuring them against.
  • Letting an open question quietly disappear once an option feels appealing.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Agree the criteria before anyone argues Families fight about places when they haven't agreed what matters. A written list of essentials and preferences, made before the comparison, gives everyone the same ruler.
  2. Separate what you saw from what you were told from how it felt A tour mixes three things: what you watched happen, what a staff member said, and the feeling you left with. All three matter. Only the first two can be checked.
  3. Keep the open questions visible Once one option feels appealing, the unanswered questions start to feel answered. Listing them, with who has to answer each, keeps them alive until someone actually does.
  4. Prepare the family conversation You're not writing the decision yet. You're writing the page that lets the family make it together: the criteria, the facts, what's still open, who needs to be present, and what to ask next.
