14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your mother is well, and nobody is choosing anything. But you've seen other families fall apart over a decision made in a week, and you'd rather the siblings agree now on how you'll decide than argue later about what.

Where they want to be

You can say what matters most to your mother, where the family agrees and where it doesn't, how you'll share information when the time comes, and what would need fresh confirmation before any real choice.

Intermediate winI can describe how our family would make a care decision for your mother, and we agreed it while nothing was at stake.
Consumer outputA one-page Family Decision Agreement draft: What matters most to your mother, What matters to each of us, How we'll share information and talk, What we'll recheck before any choice, and What we've agreed not to do yet.
Reserved for the softwareThe Care Option Decision Record, the lesson on agreeing criteria before debating names, and the documented decision process with its revisit conditions belong to the course. Helping the family work through real disagreement, keeping your mother's preferences visible when the pressure is on, and comparing actual options against her needs is Sherene's professional work.
Stop lineDo not name or favor any provider or setting, say who will hold legal authority to decide, settle a disagreement between relatives, predict your mother's needs, or produce the Care Option Decision Record.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Promising your mother, or each other, a specific place long before anyone knows what she'll need.
  • Assuming the siblings want the same things because they love the same person.
  • Leaving it unspoken who gathers information, who talks, and how the family will decide.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Put your mother's wishes on paper first The family's criteria should start with hers. If her words aren't written down, the loudest sibling's priorities will quietly become the family's.
  2. Find out where the family actually disagrees Siblings often believe they agree until the first real option appears. Collecting each person's priorities separately, then laying them side by side, surfaces the differences while they're still easy to talk about.
  3. Draft the ground rules for a future decision A process agreed in calm is easier to follow in a crisis. Who gathers information, how it's shared, who sits in the conversation, and what you won't do yet are all things you can settle now.
  4. Write the agreement to come back to This page isn't a plan for a move. It's the family's agreement about how it will decide, kept with your mother's wishes and a list of what will have to be confirmed fresh when the time comes.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father's care has already started, and you've been asking the staff for things in passing: a hand at breakfast, the cream for his heels, someone to check his pills. Some of it happens. A care-team meeting is coming and you want to arrive with more than a list in your head.

Where they want to be

You can hand the team one page that shows the daily help your father needs as you see it, what instructions already exist and who gave them, what he prefers, and what still needs a professional's answer.

Intermediate winI can show the care team what I've been asking for, where each instruction came from, and which questions are still open.
Consumer outputA one-page set of family notes for the team meeting with four headings: Daily help as we see it, Instructions already in place and their source, your father's preferences, and Questions for the team.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the Personal Care Plan for Team Review, with each care need matched to its instruction, the responsible clinician, the information to confirm, and a version and date. Sherene prepares the family's proposal before the facility meeting and carries medication, swallowing, and food-texture questions to the right clinician. The care interview produces the Family Care Profile that the proposal is built from.
Stop lineDo not write the care plan or the Personal Care Plan for Team Review, do not turn your father's preferences into instructions for staff, and do not reword, add to, or question any medication, diet, or therapy instruction.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Asking for things out loud and hoping they stick.
  • Mixing what your father prefers with what a professional has ordered.
  • Assuming the medication or therapy question you raised last month got answered.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Put your spoken requests in writing A request made at the nurses' station on a Tuesday afternoon lives in one person's memory. If that person is off on Thursday, so is the request.
  2. Separate instructions from wishes Your father liking his tea before his wash is a preference. The physiotherapist's note about how he transfers from bed is an instruction. On one page they look the same, and staff can't tell which is which unless you do.
  3. Find the questions still hanging Someone said they'd look at your father's medications after the hospital. Someone mentioned a swallowing check. You assumed it happened. Assumptions like these are the gaps a care-team meeting exists to close, but only if you bring them.
  4. Write the page you'll bring to the meeting The team will have their own plan. What they won't have is your view of your father's day, kept apart from their orders and clearly marked as notes for discussion. That page is what you're building.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom is managing at home. There's a pill organizer on the counter, a letter from the clinic somewhere, and a sheet from the physiotherapist she saw last spring. Nothing is wrong, and you'd like all of it in one place before anything is.

Where they want to be

You can open one file and see what help she gets today, every instruction with its source, what she prefers, and what a care team would need to assess fresh, with a date on it.

Intermediate winI can say where every piece of my mother's current care information came from and which of it is still current.
Consumer outputA one-page Where Things Stand Today sheet: Help she gets today, Instructions we have and where they came from, Her preferences, What a future care team would need to assess, and when it was last checked.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the Personal Care Planning Template, with care needs matched to their instructions, blanks left for decisions that can't be made yet, and triggers for professional reassessment. Sherene reviews the file when a care arrangement is being considered and takes medication, swallowing, and food-texture questions to the appropriate clinician. The care interview produces the Family Care Profile that the file grows from.
Stop lineDo not write a future care plan, decide what help Mom will need, create the Personal Care Planning Template, or change, interpret, or add to any medication or treatment instruction.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Writing a plan for care nobody has assessed yet.
  • Forgetting who gave an instruction, or when.
  • Leaving the important information in six places.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Take stock of what's scattered Care information collects in odd places: a pharmacy bag, a fridge magnet, a text from your sister. Before you can organize it you need to know what exists and where.
  2. Record each instruction with its source An instruction without a source can't be checked and can't be updated. Two years from now, nobody will remember whether the heel cream was the doctor's idea or a neighbor's.
  3. Keep today apart from tomorrow When a family has time, the temptation is to plan: she'll need help bathing, she'll need a rail, she'll need someone at night. Those may be true one day. Right now they're guesses, and a guess written into a file starts to look like a decision.
  4. Write the Where Things Stand Today page The point of the file is that someone could pick it up in two years, or in an emergency, and know what's current, what's hers, and what nobody has decided. One page does that better than a folder.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your husband moved into care a few weeks ago. The staff are kind and the activity calendar is full, but he spends most afternoons in his room and the mornings don't look anything like the ones you shared. You want the days to feel more like his.

Where they want to be

You can sit down with his carers and show them, in his words and yours, what an ordinary good day looked like, what he'd like now, and the practical help it would take, while leaving him free to say no.

Intermediate winI can describe what my husband misses, what would help him join in, and how to tell when he's choosing not to.
Consumer outputA one-page Good Day Conversation Sheet: What he's told us, Routines that matter, Activities he'd like and the help it would take, People he wants to stay close to, and How he says no.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the Good Day Plan, with meals and confirmed dietary restrictions kept separate, participation support, and the care team's agreed routines and open questions recorded over time. Sherene translates morning tea, meals, evening routines, and food preferences into the proposed plan and discusses participation support with the team, preserving his own choices. The care interview produces the Family Care Profile, where his daily life sits alongside everything else.
Stop lineDo not write the Good Day Plan, decide which activities he will attend, promise what the care team will accommodate, or interpret, change, or add to any dietary or clinical instruction.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Thinking an activity on the calendar means he can get there.
  • Leaving out the small routines that made the day feel like his.
  • Turning what the family wants for him into things he has to do.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Hear it from him first Families often answer for the person. He'd love the music group, we're sure of it. Maybe. The quickest way to find out is to ask, and to notice where you've been guessing.
  2. Map the day that used to be his The care conversation tends to be about meals, baths, and the 2 p.m. quiz. The paper with his coffee, the radio at six, the phone call to his brother on Sundays: those are what made a day familiar, and they're the first to go unnoticed.
  3. Work out what joining in would take The calendar says Bingo, 2 p.m., lounge. For your husband that may mean a reminder at 1:45, his hearing aids in, someone to walk down with him, and a chair near the door. Without that help, the calendar is a list of things happening to other people.
  4. Write the sheet for the conversation You're not writing instructions for the staff. You're starting a conversation about what they can offer and what he can choose. The wording matters: Please offer, not He must.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father lives on his own and does fine. He has his ways: the same cafe on Thursdays, the news at six, the garden before it gets hot. Nothing needs to change, and that's exactly why it's a good time to write down what he'd want kept if someday it did.

Where they want to be

You have one page, in his words wherever possible, describing what an ordinary good day holds for him, who matters in it, and how he lets people know when he'd rather not, dated so you know when to ask again.

Intermediate winI can describe the routines and people that make my father's day feel like his, and I know which parts came from him rather than from me.
Consumer outputA one-page Ordinary Day profile for your father: Mornings, Meals, Afternoons and activities, People, Evenings and sleep, How he says no, with the date it was written and a date to check it again.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the full Good Day Plan, with meals and any confirmed restrictions kept separate, participation support described, future accommodations left open for a provider discussion, and a process for revisiting choices. Sherene brings the profile into the proposed plan when a care arrangement is being considered, preserving your father's own choices. The care interview produces the Family Care Profile, which holds his daily life alongside his health, home, and support.
Stop lineDo not write the Good Day Plan, decide what a future provider will accommodate, plan activities for your father, or record anything about diet or medication beyond his own stated preferences.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Writing down only the practical things, like meals and medications.
  • Forgetting the small routines that make a day feel familiar.
  • Treating what he likes today as fixed for good.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Get ready for a conversation, not a form Nobody opens up to a checklist. The best material comes from stories: what he did this morning, who he ran into, what he'd never give up. Good questions get you there.
  2. Turn the conversation into a routine map After the talk you'll have stories, half-sentences, and a few surprises. Sorting them while they're fresh keeps his version from blending into yours.
  3. Notice what you've only written as tasks Left to ourselves, we write care plans about meals, pills, and showers. Those matter. But a day made only of tasks isn't a day he'd recognize. This prompt looks for the life in between.
  4. Write the Ordinary Day page, with a date on it Preferences change. The cafe closes, a friend moves, he discovers he likes the radio after all. A page with a date and a check-again line is honest about that. A page without one quietly becomes a rule.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom has carers now, or she's in a facility, and there's a plan on paper. You can't be there every day. When you ask how things are going, the answer is “fine,” and you've started to wonder what fine is based on.

Where they want to be

You can name the handful of things you're watching, say who sees each one and where the record is, point to who's following up on every concern, and admit out loud which parts of Mom's care nobody is checking.

Intermediate winI can say what I'm watching in Mom's care, who can actually see it, and which of my concerns has nobody following up.
Consumer outputA one-page Watch List: What we're watching and what we'd see, Who can see it, What we have no way to know yet, Concerns and who owns them, and Questions for the care team.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the Care Monitoring and Response Plan: each item with its definition, baseline, information source, agreed review frequency, what prompts contact, and the person or service to call, with clinical warning signs and response instructions confirmed by the responsible clinician. Sherene turns the wish to measure care into an agreed monitoring plan with the care team. The care interview produces the Family Care Profile the plan refers back to.
Stop lineDo not build the Care Monitoring and Response Plan, set any clinical threshold, warning sign, or response instruction, assess whether Mom is safe, or judge the quality of the care she is getting.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Tracking everything, so nothing gets looked at.
  • Hearing nothing and taking it as good news.
  • Collecting worries without deciding who follows up on each.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Choose a few things worth watching A family that tracks everything ends up with a notebook nobody reads. Monitoring works when each thing you watch connects to something in the plan and someone could actually see it.
  2. Work out who can actually see each thing You can't watch what you're not there for. Carers' notes, a facility chart, a neighbor who pops in: each sees something different, and some things no one you know can see. Silence from those places isn't reassurance. It's a blank.
  3. Give every concern an owner Worries pile up: the cold lunch, the missed shower, the bruise nobody explained. Each got mentioned to someone. Few got assigned. A concern without an owner is just a worry with a date on it.
  4. Write the Watch List The care team will have its own monitoring. Yours is different: a few things you're watching, where the information comes from, and an honest list of what you can't see. That's what you take to the next conversation.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife is well, or well enough that nothing has to be decided. You've started thinking about a day when other people are involved in her care, and about how you'd know whether that care was going the way it should. You don't have a provider, and you don't need one yet.

Where they want to be

You have a plain description of her ordinary week today, a realistic list of who could keep an eye on things, and the questions you'd ask any future care team about sharing information and responding to a concern. The clinical thresholds stay blank, on purpose.

Intermediate winI can describe what's normal for my wife this year, who could realistically notice a change, and what I'd need to agree with a future care team before monitoring means anything.
Consumer outputA one-page Starting Point sheet: What an ordinary week looks like now, Who could keep an eye on things and what they'd see, Questions for a future care team, What we won't decide ourselves, and When we'll look at this again.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the blank Care Monitoring and Response Plan template: items, what can be observed, who records it, information source, review frequency, what prompts contact, response contacts, and follow-up owner, with clinical thresholds left for a clinician and a plan for when monitoring is activated. Sherene turns the family's observations into an agreed monitoring plan when a care arrangement is in view, with medical thresholds confirmed by the responsible clinician. The care interview produces the Family Care Profile that any future plan starts from.
Stop lineDo not build the monitoring template or tracker, define what counts as normal or abnormal for your wife, invent warning signs or thresholds, or decide when monitoring should begin.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Inventing warning signs and thresholds no clinician has set.
  • Building a tracker that nobody has agreed to fill in.
  • Assuming a future provider will tell you things without being asked.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Write down this year's normal A year from now, someone may ask, is this new? You'll want to answer from notes, not memory. What's normal for your wife today is the most useful thing you can record, and it's the one thing only you can.
  2. Find out who could realistically notice A tracker with no one to fill it in is a good intention. Before deciding what to watch, work out who is actually around, how often, and whether they'd be willing to write anything down.
  3. List what you'd need to agree with a future care team Families assume a provider will share notes, call when something's off, and know who to call. Some do, some don't, and none of it is automatic. Knowing the questions now means you ask them before signing, not after.
  4. Write the Starting Point sheet What you've made isn't a monitoring plan, and it shouldn't pretend to be. It's a starting point: today's normal, the people around her, the questions for later, and a clear statement of what you're leaving to professionals.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Dad is moving to a new care setting, or a new caregiver is starting at the house, and the date is close. Someone asked for “the paperwork” and you aren't sure what that includes or who is bringing the walker.

Where they want to be

You can say what has been requested, what is in hand, what is only assumed, and who is handling each piece.

Intermediate winI can see every transition task in one place, with a name beside it and the gaps marked.
Consumer outputA one-page readiness list: Requested by the provider, In hand, Still missing, Who is handling it, and Questions for the provider.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the full Care Transition Preparation Pack, including the care-plan proposal, equipment confirmations with the right professionals, and the final pre-transition review. Sherene helps the family get the paperwork done and shares out the load when she is part of the engagement.
Stop lineDo not create the Care Transition Preparation Pack, decide whether the move should go ahead, judge whether the new setting or caregiver is suitable, or tell the family which equipment Dad needs.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Scrambling for records at the last minute.
  • Assuming the equipment and supplies have been arranged.
  • Leaving one relative to manage every task.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Turn the provider's request into a plain checklist The provider's list arrives as a form, a phone call, or a sentence at the end of an email. Until it is written in plain words, you can't tell what you have and what you don't.
  2. Separate what's arranged from what's assumed Somebody said the hospital bed was ordered. Somebody heard the agency brings the supplies. Each of those is a sentence, not a delivery. The gap between them shows up on moving day.
  3. Share the work before one person carries it In most families, the tasks drift to whoever is closest or most organized. By the move date that person is exhausted and the others feel shut out.
  4. Build your one-page readiness list With a date approaching, you need something you can read in a minute and hand to a sibling. Not a binder. One page.

Where they are

Your mother is doing fine at home, and nothing is planned. You've noticed that if a new caregiver started next month, the information they'd need is in six places and two people's heads.

Where they want to be

You can point to one file that holds what any new caregiver would need to know, with the open items clearly marked as waiting on a provider and a date that don't exist yet.

Intermediate winI can hand someone one file about my mother's care and know what still has to wait.
Consumer outputA one-page readiness file: Current care information, Where each piece lives, Depends on a future provider, Who could help later, and Review date.
Reserved for the softwareThe course turns the file into the full Transition-Readiness File and Future Handoff Template, including the care-plan proposal and the belongings and transport plan. Sherene reviews what the family has gathered and helps distribute the work when a transition becomes real.
Stop lineDo not treat the file as a decision that your mother will move, suggest a type of setting or a timeline, create the Care Transition Preparation Pack, or assess whether home is safe for her.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Waiting until a move is urgent to organize records.
  • Handing out tasks without checking whether people can actually do them.
  • Mistaking a preparation file for a decision to move.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Map where the information lives today You know where most things are. The trouble is that “you know” is the storage system, and it doesn't transfer well when you're busy or away.
  2. Mark what has to wait for a provider Some of the file can be finished now. Some of it can't be finished until there is an actual provider with actual forms. Mixing the two makes the file feel permanently incomplete.
  3. Check who could help, without signing anyone up It's tempting to pencil in names now. But a brother who said “sure” at Thanksgiving may have a new job by the time anything happens. This is about possibilities, not commitments.
  4. Assemble the readiness file A file that lives in a folder on your desk gets opened. A file that lives in your memory and three email threads does not.

Where they are

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming the receiving team has every document.
  • Not knowing whom to contact.
  • Losing early concerns in separate family messages.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Check what was actually received, not just sent You gave the folder to someone at the front desk. That is not the same as the nurse having his medication list. Sent and received are two different columns.
  2. Sort out who to call about what In the first week you meet a dozen people and remember three. When something seems off at 7 p.m., you need to know which of them to call, and who covers when they're off.
  3. Pull the family's concerns into one list Your daughter noticed he wasn't wearing his glasses. Your son thinks dinner was late. You wondered about the night shift. Each worry is real, and each one is in a different thread.
  4. Write the first-days log Everything so far lives in three tables. The family needs one page they can all read, and you need something to carry into the first care-plan meeting.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Dad doesn't need a new care arrangement, and this isn't about choosing one. You've watched a friend go through an admission day in a blur and would rather know what to ask before you're standing in a hallway with a clipboard.

Where they want to be

You have a short, reusable set of questions and a family communication plan, with clear blanks for the contacts and schedules that only a real provider can supply.

Intermediate winI know what we'd ask on day one and who in the family would keep everyone informed.
Consumer outputA one-page first-days template: Questions for any provider before arrival, Contact fields to fill in later, Family update plan, and Not known until a provider is chosen.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the full admission-day and first-days template with an owner, the discrepancy record, and the care-plan meeting preparation. Sherene helps the family through the actual move or start of care when she is part of the engagement, and she knows which questions matter for a given kind of provider.
Stop lineDo not pick a provider or a type of care setting, fill in contacts or schedules the family doesn't have, create the Admission and First-Days Action Log, or imply that a move is coming because the template exists.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Trying to learn the process during a stressful arrival.
  • Assuming every provider follows the same process.
  • Forgetting to plan how the family will stay in touch.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Draft the questions you'd ask any provider On the day, people hand you forms and you sign them. The questions come to you that night. Writing them down now, with no pressure, means you'll have them when it counts.
  2. Mark what changes from one provider to the next A friend's experience with one agency is not a map for another. Some things are the same everywhere. Many are not, and a template that pretends otherwise will mislead you.
  3. Decide how the family will stay in touch When something finally happens, the person on the spot gets fifteen texts asking the same thing. A plan made now, when nobody is upset, saves that.
  4. Put the template together A template is only useful if you can find it and trust it. One page, clearly labeled as unfinished on purpose, does the job.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife has moved, or a new caregiver has taken over at home. You sent a folder and told two people about her mornings. You're not sure anyone read the folder, and this morning went badly.

Where they want to be

You can list what the receiving team needs, show what they've confirmed and what they haven't, and name who is sorting out each piece that doesn't match.

Intermediate winI know what the new team has in hand, what they have only been sent, and what still conflicts.
Consumer outputA one-page handoff record: What the team must know, Sent and to whom, Receipt confirmed, Conflicting or unclear items, and Who is following up.
Reserved for the softwareThe course completes the Care Transition Handoff Packet and Receipt Log, including the care-plan proposal with its review status, sourced clinical instructions, and the versioned packet. Sherene bridges what the family knows at home to the receiving community or caregiver and sends her care-plan proposal when she is part of the engagement.
Stop lineDo not create the Handoff Packet and Receipt Log, resolve conflicting medical or care instructions, judge whether the new team is caring for her properly, or write clinical instructions the family hasn't received from a clinician.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming a sent document was reviewed.
  • Losing her personal routines in the transfer.
  • Leaving conflicting information without an owner.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Write down what only you know about her The medical chart travels. The fact that she likes the curtains open and panics if the radio is off does not, unless you write it. These details are what make the first weeks go well or badly.
  2. List what the receiving team must have Some of what you know came from her doctor. Some came from the last aide. Some you worked out yourself. The team needs to know which is which, and so do you.
  3. Separate what was sent from what was received An email that nobody opened has not arrived. When the team does something different from what you sent, that is information, not an accusation. It tells you where to look.
  4. Assemble the handoff record You now have three tables and a page about her. The record pulls them into one sheet that shows what is settled and what still has no owner.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

You've been caring for someone for a while and you carry most of it in your head. Nothing is changing, but you've wondered what would happen if you were sick for a week and a stranger had to step in.

Where they want to be

You have one packet, dated, that a new caregiver could read, with a note on who may see it and when it was last checked.

Intermediate winI can hand a new caregiver one dated packet instead of explaining everything from memory.
Consumer outputA one-page packet index: About them, Current instructions and their sources, Retired or unsure, Who may receive this, and Version and review date.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the full versioned Handoff Packet and Receipt Log, including the care-plan proposal and the receipt-confirmation process for when it is used. Sherene reviews what the family has captured and, when she is part of the engagement, bridges it to a future community or caregiver.
Stop lineDo not create the Handoff Packet and Receipt Log, mark any handoff as having happened, decide who legally may receive information, write or update care instructions, or suggest that a change in caregiver is needed.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Reconstructing the routine in a crisis instead of writing it down now.
  • Keeping outdated instructions mixed in with current ones.
  • Assuming everyone may receive the same information.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Capture the routine while nothing is wrong The best time to describe how the day works is a day when it works. Trying to remember it from a hospital waiting room is how details get lost.
  2. Sort current instructions from old ones Over months and years, instructions pile up. The one from two doctors ago sits next to last week's. A new caregiver can't tell them apart, and in a hurry, neither can you.
  3. Think through who may receive what A paid aide, a neighbor who checks in, and a sibling across the country do not all need the same packet. Deciding this now avoids an awkward choice made in a rush.
  4. Set up the packet index A packet without a date and a version is just a pile of paper with a nicer name. The index is what makes it trustworthy a year from now.

Where they are

Your father's care arrangement grew one favor at a time. Your sister handles the pharmacy, a neighbor drives, you call the facility, and nobody is sure who follows up when something changes. Last week a task went unhandled because everyone thought someone else had it.

Where they want to be

You can name who does each task today, which tasks have no owner, and which questions need a clinician rather than a family coordinator.

Intermediate winI can see every task in your father's care, who actually does it, and where the gaps and the overload are.

Sherene coordinates with facility staff, nursing, and physicians, defines her own role, and checks whether one person is becoming overwhelmed.
Stop lineDo not assign tasks to relatives who have not agreed to them, decide who holds decision authority for your father, judge whether the current arrangement is safe, or create the Family and Professional Care Team Plan.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming someone else has a task covered.
  • Treating the family coordinator as the clinical decision-maker.
  • Letting all the follow-up land on one tired person.

The prompts, one job each

  1. List everyone and what they actually do Care arrangements grow by favors. After a few months nobody has a complete list, and the person who thinks they know is usually missing someone.
  2. Find the tasks nobody owns The task that went wrong last week probably didn't belong to anyone. Listing the work separately from the people shows you the holes.
  3. Check what is landing on one person Usually one person is quietly carrying most of it, and they may not say so. Seeing the hours in a list is often the first time anyone, including that person, notices.
  4. Sort the questions by who should answer them A family coordinator can arrange rides and track paperwork. They cannot change a medication or decide a treatment. Mixing those up is how families get hurt and how clinicians stop returning calls.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom is managing fine, and the family has started saying things like 'we'll all pitch in when the time comes.' Nobody has said what that means, who lives close enough to do what, or who would keep track of it all. You have time to find out.

Where they want to be

You can describe who in the family could realistically take which role, what has actually been promised, and who would hold the plan until it's needed.

Intermediate winI can tell the difference between help my family has offered and help my family has agreed to, and I know who holds the plan.
Consumer outputA one-page provisional care team map: People Who Could Be Involved, Confirmed Commitments, Offers Not Yet Confirmed, Roles Nobody Has Claimed, and Who Keeps This Current.
Reserved for the softwareThe course leads the actual family conversation about future roles, records commitments against each person's capacity, raises the healthcare representative question for proper clarification, and sets the conditions for confirming or updating the plan; the Family and Professional Care Team Plan is its deliverable. Sherene defines the professional roles that would need confirming and checks whether the proposed arrangement would leave one person overwhelmed.
Stop lineDo not assign future roles to relatives who have not agreed, treat an offer as a commitment, decide who should hold decision authority for Mom, or create the Family and Professional Care Team Plan.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Expecting siblings to share the work without being asked.
  • Letting people promise more help than they can give.
  • Relying on one coordinator with no one behind them.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Map who could be involved, honestly Families picture the future team as 'all of us.' Written down, it is usually three people within an hour's drive and four who love her from far away. Both groups matter, but they can't do the same things.
  2. Separate what's promised from what's possible 'Of course I'll help' is kind, and it isn't a plan. The useful question is what, specifically, and whether that still fits when someone has a full-time job and two kids.
  3. Give far-away family something real to carry Distance is the most common reason everything lands on the sibling nearby. The nearby sibling resents it, the distant one feels useless, and both are right. There is plenty of coordination work a phone can do.
  4. Put it on one page and name who keeps it current A plan nobody maintains is wrong by the time you need it. One person should hold it, and one person should be able to take over if they can't.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife's care now passes between you, your daughter, a home aide, and the clinic. Last week you told someone about a change and found out later it never reached the person who needed it. Everyone is sending messages; nobody is sure who is holding the ball.

Where they want to be

You can explain what went wrong with a recent handoff, describe the updates that happen every week, and send one message that says what changed, what's needed, and who owns it.

Intermediate winI can write an update the next person can actually act on, and I know which of my messages are still unanswered.
Consumer outputA one-page handoff sheet: Updates That Recur, Our Handoff Message Format, Sent and Waiting for Acknowledgment, and Unanswered Items.
Reserved for the softwareThe course agrees the sender, receiver, and channel for each type of update with the provider and the family, uses the format on a live handoff, and records acknowledgment and ownership for follow-up; the Care Communication and Handoff Protocol is its deliverable. Sherene applies her approach to the left-hand, right-hand problem across shifts, siblings, and backup caregivers, and works within the provider's own communication process.
Stop lineDo not decide what clinical information a provider must act on, tell the family which of the provider's channels to use without the provider being asked, settle who was at fault for a missed message, or create the Care Communication and Handoff Protocol.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming the message got to the right person.
  • Repeating the same update without ever writing down the decision.
  • Letting a task vanish between one caregiver and the next.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Take apart one message that didn't land The fastest way to fix handoffs is to look closely at one that failed. Not to blame anyone. To see where the information stopped.
  2. List the updates that happen every week Some handoffs are one-offs. Most repeat: the aide tells you how the morning went, you tell your daughter before her turn, someone calls the clinic back. Those are the ones worth building a habit around.
  3. Write one handoff that names an owner 'FYI, she didn't eat much today' is information. 'She didn't eat much today, can you watch dinner and let me know' is a handoff. The difference is a receiver and an owner.
  4. Build your one-page handoff sheet Once you can see the recurring updates and have a format that works, you need somewhere to track what's been sent and what's still hanging. That is what keeps responsibility from disappearing.

  9. Record unconfirmed or unanswered handoffs.
  10. Review how backup caregivers receive the current information.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your brother coordinates most of what Mom needs, and he does it well. He also does it from memory. Nothing urgent is happening, but if he were out of reach for a week, nobody else would know where to start. You have time to change that.

Where they want to be

You can say what information a backup would need, what a standard update should contain, and where the current plan will be kept so anyone with permission can find it.

Intermediate winI can see what lives only in the coordinator's head, and I know what we'd need to write down before a backup could step in.
Consumer outputA one-page readiness sheet: What the Coordinator Knows, Our Update Format, Where the Current Plan Lives, and What a Backup Would Still Be Missing.
Reserved for the softwareThe course agrees the channel and plan location with the family, asks the provider which contacts to use, and rehearses a coordinator absence with a de-identified example, then fixes the gaps the rehearsal exposes; the Care Communication and Handoff Protocol is its deliverable. Sherene applies the same handoff principle across siblings and backup caregivers and advises on how the family's system should meet the provider's.
Stop lineDo not choose a channel or tool for the family, decide who the backup coordinator will be, tell the family how a provider wants to be contacted, or create the Care Communication and Handoff Protocol.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Keeping the whole plan in one person's memory.
  • Trusting a group text to make ownership clear.
  • Explaining the routine only when the coordinator is already gone.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Write down what the coordinator carries in their head The coordinator knows the pharmacy's hours, which neighbor has a key, and that Mom won't take pills from a stranger. None of that is written anywhere. Getting it onto paper is the first step, and the coordinator is the only one who can do it.
  2. Decide what every update should include If each update has the same shape, a backup can read the last few and catch up. If each one is a free-form text, they have to read everything and still guess.
  3. Pick where the current plan will live, and who can get to it A plan that's in three email threads and a drawer is not a shared plan. The question isn't which app. It's whether the backup could find the current version at eleven at night without calling anyone.
  4. See what a backup would still be missing You won't know what's missing until you imagine someone stepping in. You don't need to stage a real absence to do that on paper. The real rehearsal comes later.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your husband has been in the facility three weeks, and the care-plan meeting is next Tuesday. You have a list of things you asked for in the first week, a copy of something the staff called the care plan, and no idea which of your requests actually made it in.

Where they want to be

You can name your top priorities for him, point to where each one does or doesn't appear in the provider's written plan, and leave the meeting with every item marked agreed, deferred, or open, with a name next to it.

Intermediate winI know which of my requests are in the plan, which aren't, and which questions are mine to ask versus a clinician's to answer.
Consumer outputA one-page meeting record, ready to fill in: Our Priorities, Where the Plan Addresses Them, Questions to Ask, Decisions for the Clinicians, and Agreed, Deferred, or Open with Owner and Date.
Reserved for the softwareThe course prepares the family's priority questions alongside the personal care proposal and About Me profile, works through differences and practical constraints with the provider, and documents accepted, deferred, and declined requests and how changes enter the provider's plan; the Care-Plan Alignment and Meeting Record is its deliverable. Sherene attends the first care-plan meeting when it's in scope, compares the family's proposal with the interdisciplinary plan, and records what has been addressed and what remains open.
Stop lineDo not interpret the provider's clinical plan or restate it as settled fact, decide which side is right where the family and provider differ, judge the quality of the facility's care, or create the Care-Plan Alignment and Meeting Record.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Assuming that because you asked, it's in the plan.
  • Leaving the meeting without names and dates on the follow-up.
  • Hearing every 'no' as a personal fight.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Put your priorities in order You'll get a limited amount of time in the room. If everything is a priority, the staff will pick what to address, and it may not be what matters most to him.
  2. Compare your list with what's written in their plan Asking for something and having it written into the plan are different things. The plan is what the staff on the next shift will read. If it's not there, it isn't happening reliably.
  3. Separate a question from a disagreement Most of what feels like a fight is a question nobody has answered. Some differences are real and have reasons. Knowing which is which keeps the meeting about him.
  4. Set up the record you'll fill in at the meeting The meeting will move fast. If the page you're writing on already has the right columns, you'll leave with owners and dates. If it's blank, you'll leave with a feeling.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father lives at home and nothing has changed. You've heard that if he ever moves into care there will be 'care-plan meetings,' and you don't know what one is, who comes, or what a family is supposed to bring. You'd rather learn the shape of it now than in the hallway afterward.

Where they want to be

You can explain in plain words what a care-plan meeting is for, have an agenda and notes template ready to adapt, and know the difference between a family preference and a clinical decision.

Intermediate winI understand how a care-plan meeting works, I have a template ready, and I know which of our wishes are requests rather than instructions.
Consumer outputA one-page meeting preparation kit: How These Meetings Usually Work, Our Reusable Agenda, Our Father's Preferences as Questions, and a Blank Record for Requests, Decisions, and Follow-Up.
Reserved for the softwareThe course works through practice examples with provider decisions left open, plans who asks and who records, and teaches how family requests become documented actions once there is a real provider and a real plan; the Care-Plan Alignment and Meeting Record is its deliverable. Sherene's attendance at an actual meeting, her comparison of the family's proposal with a provider's interdisciplinary plan, and her read on what remains open are professional work for when the time comes.
Stop lineDo not describe what any particular provider's plan will contain, present your father's preferences as instructions a provider must follow, fill in decisions no provider has made, or create the Care-Plan Alignment and Meeting Record.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Learning what a care-plan meeting is at your first one.
  • Expecting the family's wishes to become clinical orders on their own.
  • Not deciding in advance how decisions will get written down.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Learn what these meetings are for, in plain words A care-plan meeting is a routine part of facility and home-care life, but most families meet their first one unprepared. Knowing the general shape, who's usually there and what they're trying to do, takes most of the fear out of it.
  2. Draft an agenda you can reuse An agenda is the family's way of making sure its questions get time. Build it once, generically, and you can adapt it in ten minutes when a real meeting is called.
  3. Turn his preferences into questions, not instructions 'Dad never wants to be woken before eight' is a preference. Whether a care setting can honor it depends on staffing, safety, and his condition at the time. Writing it as a question respects both him and the people who will care for him.
  4. Practice recording requests, decisions, and follow-up The habit that matters most in these meetings is writing down what was actually decided, separately from what was asked. Practicing on a made-up example now means you won't be learning it during the real thing.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Dad has had home care for six weeks and you're not there most days. Your sister says it's going fine, your brother thinks the aide skips things, and both of them are going on feeling. Nobody has looked at what the plan actually says.

Where they want to be

You can say, item by item, what the plan promised, what someone actually saw and when, and what no one has checked yet.

Intermediate winI can separate what I've seen from what I feel, and I know which parts of Dad's care nobody has looked at.
Consumer outputA one-page care review: What the plan says, What we've seen (with dates), What we haven't seen, and Who follows up.
Reserved for the softwareThe course teaches the full Family Care Review Dashboard, including the person's own experience of the care, provider reports gathered through agreed channels, confirmed-or-unconfirmed status for each item, and the check on whether the family's monitoring load is sustainable. Sherene reads the review, weighs what the discrepancies mean, and brings them to the care team within her professional scope.
Stop lineDo not judge whether the care is adequate or safe, declare that an aide or agency is failing, set a threshold for when to escalate, or build the Family Care Review Dashboard.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Going on a feeling that things are fine.
  • Treating a gap in your notes as proof of good or bad care.
  • Collecting worries without checking what was actually agreed.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Turn the plan into a list you can check Most families have never read the care plan as a checklist. It reads as a description of help, not as a set of specific things that should happen on specific days. Until it is a list, you can't compare anything to it.
  2. Sort what you've seen by date and source Your sense that things are fine, or not fine, is made of a few real observations and a lot of impression. Pulling them apart is uncomfortable and useful. An observation with a date can be discussed; a feeling can only be argued about.
  3. Line the two up and mark the empty spaces When no one was there to see a task happen, the honest answer is 'not observed.' It's not evidence the aide skipped it, and it's not evidence she did it. Families fall both ways, depending on their mood.
  4. Put it on one page with a name beside each follow-up A review with no owner is a list of complaints. The point of writing a name beside each open item is that it stops being a feeling in the family and becomes a question someone will actually ask.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your mother lives on her own and is doing well. You've started talking as a family about what help might look like someday, and you've realized none of you would know how to tell whether a care plan was being followed. There's no rush, which is exactly why this is a good time.

Where they want to be

You have a practice review template your family has tried once on a fictional scenario, with names beside the jobs and a clear list of what you'd need to ask a provider for.

Intermediate winI can show my family what a care review would compare, who could realistically do the watching, and what we'd have to ask a provider for.
Consumer outputA one-page practice review template with headings What we'd compare, Who could gather it, How we'll keep unknowns visible, and Questions for a future provider.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the full Family Care Review Dashboard and rehearses it with a labeled scenario, including the person's experience, confirmed-or-unconfirmed status, follow-up owners, and the check on whether the monitoring load is fair across the family. Sherene helps the family settle realistic roles and tells them which review and information-access arrangements to confirm with a provider when care begins.
Stop lineDo not invent provider data or access the family doesn't have, decide what level of oversight your mother will need, rate any type of care setting, or produce the Family Care Review Dashboard.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Designing a dashboard before anyone has agreed what it should show.
  • Assuming you'll be handed provider records later.
  • Letting the whole review job land on one relative.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Decide what a review would actually compare A review compares what was agreed with what happened. Families who skip the first half end up with a notebook of visits and nothing to hold them against. Agreeing what you'd compare is the whole foundation.
  2. Try the review on a made-up week You learn what a review feels like by filling one in, not by reading about it. A fictional week with gaps in it shows the family how much stays unknown even when everyone is paying attention.
  3. Work out who could gather what Review work tends to fall on whoever lives closest, and it stays there until that person burns out. Listing the jobs separately from the people lets the family see the load before anyone is carrying it.
  4. Draft the template and the provider questions Families assume they will see the aide's notes or the residence's records. Often they won't, or not without asking. The questions about access belong on paper now, so they get asked on day one instead of month three.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife moved into a care residence two months ago. Three times now you've arrived to find something that bothered you, and the last time you said more than you meant to at the front desk. Nothing has changed, and you're not sure what you actually asked for.

Where they want to be

You can walk in with two or three dated examples, a named person to speak to, one clear request, and a page to write their answer on.

Intermediate winI can say exactly what I saw, when, and what I'm asking for, to the right person, in a tone I won't regret.
Consumer outputA one-page concern sheet: What I observed (with dates), How it connects to her plan, Who I'm asking, What I'm asking for, and Their response and next date.
Reserved for the softwareThe course teaches the full Care Concern and Escalation Log, including the immediate-help route, the agreed escalation path, response tracking, and keeping the person's own perspective in the record. Sherene helps with the difficult conversations themselves, with disagreements between relatives, and with recognizing when an issue belongs with a clinician, provider leadership, or another professional rather than with coaching.
Stop lineDo not decide whether your wife is safe or her care is adequate, judge the residence or its staff, tell the family when a concern must be escalated, or produce the Care Concern and Escalation Log.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Frustration standing in for specific examples.
  • Repeating the complaint without asking for a particular response.
  • An open issue that nobody is clearly responsible for following.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Turn the frustration into dated examples When you're upset, the facts and the feelings come out in one breath, and staff hear the feelings. Separating them doesn't make the feelings wrong. It makes the facts usable.
  2. Work out what kind of concern this is and who it belongs to One frustration is often three different issues: a task not done, a message not passed on, and a question only a nurse can answer. Each goes to a different person. If you believe your wife is in danger right now, this guide is not the route; call the nurse on duty or emergency services.
  3. Write a request that asks for a specific answer A complaint invites an apology. A request invites an answer. The difference is one sentence at the end that says what you want and asks when you'll hear back.
  4. Set up the page that keeps the issue alive Issues don't get resolved or refused so much as forgotten. A page with a response box, a name, and a check-back date is the simplest way to make sure yours doesn't fade.

Draft written 2026-10-02 for review.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your husband is doing fine, and you've never had to challenge a nurse, an aide, or a doctor about anything. You know that if care ever becomes part of your lives, you'd rather know how to say something than find out in the middle of being upset.

Where they want to be

You've practiced one factual concern message, your family has agreed how to tell each other when something seems off, and you have a blank contact plan ready to fill in the day care starts.

Intermediate winI can describe a concern in facts and dates, and my family knows how we'll raise worries with each other before we take them anywhere else.
Consumer outputA one-page advocacy practice sheet: How we describe a concern, How we raise it with each other, A practice script, and Contacts to confirm when care begins.
Reserved for the softwareThe course rehearses the full Care Concern and Escalation Log, including separating emergency routes from routine contacts, documenting responses, and tracking an unresolved issue to its owner. Sherene coaches the real conversations when they come, helps with tension between relatives and with staff, and tells the family when a matter belongs with a clinician or provider leadership rather than with her.
Stop lineDo not decide what would count as a problem in your husband's future care, judge any kind of provider, set rules for when to escalate, or build the Care Concern and Escalation Log.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Waiting for a real conflict to learn the process.
  • Believing that being polite means saying nothing.
  • Expecting a consultant or a support group to be on call around the clock.

The prompts, one job each

  1. See the difference between a complaint and a concern Most of us have only ever complained. A concern is a different thing: dates, what was seen, who saw it, and the part of the plan it touches. Seeing the two side by side teaches more than any list of rules.
  2. Agree how your family will raise a worry with each other Before anyone speaks to a provider, the family has to agree what it's asking for. Families that skip this send three relatives with three different messages, and staff stop listening to all of them.
  3. Write a short script you could use with any provider Polite and clear are not opposites. A script you've said aloud once at the kitchen table is the thing that lets you be both when it matters.
  4. Prepare the contact plan you'll fill in later You can't know the names yet. You can know the blanks. A page that already asks who the routine contact is, who covers nights, and how concerns are heard means you'll ask on the first day instead of the first bad day.

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father's care plan was written in the spring. Since then his walking has gotten worse, his morning aide gave notice, and he's started refusing the day program. Everyone agrees things have changed. Nobody has written down what, and your brother is still working from the old plan.

Where they want to be

You can hand the care team a dated list of what's changed, know which items need their review before anything is altered, and know who in the family tells whom once decisions are made.

Intermediate winI can name what has changed about my father's situation, with dates, and tell which changes need a professional's review before we act.
Consumer outputA one-page change list: What's changed (with dates), What part of the plan it touches, What needs professional review, and Who needs to know.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the full Care Plan Review and Change Log, including the provider's actual review process and schedule, recorded decisions and who authorized them, document versions, and the next review trigger. Sherene prepares the family for the care-plan review or attends it, adjusts the family's proposal as needs shift, and confirms the review timing for the real setting instead of a remembered rule.
Stop lineDo not decide whether your father's care should change, propose new instructions or medication adjustments, state that a move is needed, or produce the Care Plan Review and Change Log.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Still acting on assumptions from when the plan was written.
  • Changing how things are done without the right review.
  • Updating your copy while the rest of the team uses another.

The prompts, one job each

  1. List what's actually different since the plan was written Everyone in the family knows something has changed, and everyone means something slightly different. Writing the changes down with dates turns 'he's declining' into a list the care team can respond to.
  2. Trace each change to the part of the plan it touches A plan goes out of date one line at a time. Finding the exact lines that no longer describe your father, and the changes the plan never anticipated, tells you what the review actually has to cover.
  3. Separate what needs a professional from what the family can handle Some changes are logistics: who drives on Thursdays now that the aide is leaving. Others touch his health or the instructions in his plan, and those need the people responsible for them to look first. Mixing the two leads families to change things they shouldn't, or wait on things they needn't.
  4. Put the changes and the messengers on one page The most common failure here is quiet: one relative updates a document, the aide keeps following the old one, and nobody notices for weeks. Naming who tells whom is how the whole team ends up on the same page.

Draft written 2026-10-02 for review.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

You've got a first version of a care plan for the person you're caring for, and that already feels like an achievement. Nothing is pressing. But plans go stale, and nobody has said who will keep this one current or what would make you look at it again.

Where they want to be

You can say which changes would bring your family back to the plan, when you'll look at it anyway, who holds the current version, and which review questions are still waiting for a provider.

Intermediate winI can name the changes that would make us revisit the plan, and my family knows who keeps the current copy.
Consumer outputA one-page review readiness sheet: What would trigger a review, Our family review dates, Who keeps the current version, and Provider review requirements to confirm.
Reserved for the softwareThe course builds the full Care Plan Review and Change Log with a versioned template, recorded decisions, the trigger list for seeking updated professional advice, and the discipline of keeping unverified provider requirements marked open. Sherene helps the family set a realistic review rhythm, adjusts the family's proposal as priorities shift, and confirms actual review schedules for whatever setting is eventually chosen.
Stop lineDo not invent a required review schedule, decide which changes would mean a different level of care or a move, predict the course of a condition, or produce the Care Plan Review and Change Log.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Treating the first plan as the final one.
  • Making up a required review schedule that no provider ever set.
  • Leaving it unclear who is responsible for updates.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Name the changes that would send you back to the plan A plan doesn't announce when it has gone out of date. The family has to decide in advance what kinds of change would mean 'look at this again,' and write them in words two relatives would both recognize.
  2. Set a family review rhythm that fits real life Families either never review the plan or invent a strict schedule they've heard somewhere and then feel guilty about missing. A modest rhythm you'll actually keep beats a rule you'll abandon by summer.
  3. Pick who holds the current version, and a backup If nobody owns the document, everybody has a slightly different copy. If one person owns it with no backup, the plan disappears the week they get sick. Both are easy to prevent now.
  4. Write the sheet and the questions for a future provider Some review dates will come from a provider you haven't chosen yet, and you can't know them now. You can leave labeled blanks so the family never mistakes a guess for a requirement.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Sherene has been coordinating your father's care since he moved, and she has said the time is coming for the family to take more of it on. You've sat in the meetings, but you couldn't write down what she actually does in a week.

Where they want to be

You can name the recurring tasks behind your father's care, say which ones someone in the family has done rather than watched, and bring an honest list of where you'd want help to the handoff conversation.

Intermediate winI can list what has been done for your father's care each week, say which parts my family has actually done ourselves, and say where we would want help.
Consumer outputA one-page handoff starting list with four headings: Tasks we've seen, Tasks we've done ourselves, Tasks we'd want help with, and Questions for the handoff conversation.
Reserved for the softwareThe Family Training course walks the family through the operating routine, rehearses the care-review checklist, meeting preparation, and concern logging with a lead and a backup, and builds the Family Care Management Playbook. Sherene judges which responsibilities are ready to transfer and agrees the handoff status with the family.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Care Management Playbook, judge whether the family is ready, decide which responsibilities transfer, or treat a written list as proof that anyone can do the task.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Relying on memory for things nobody wrote down.
  • Treating watching Sherene as the same as doing it.
  • Agreeing to take on tasks the family is not ready for.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Write down what has been happening each week When someone else coordinates well, the work disappears. You remember the big meetings and forget the twenty phone calls that made them go smoothly.
  2. Separate what you've done from what you've watched Sitting in a care meeting is not the same as running one. Families often believe they know a task because they have seen it done many times.
  3. Spot where you would want help The pressure in a handoff is to say yes to everything. A family that can point to the tasks it is unsure about is in a stronger position than one that nods along.
  4. Put it on one page for the handoff conversation Sherene can only help with what she can see. One page that shows where the family stands lets her spend the meeting on the real questions instead of reconstructing them.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom runs her own life. She drives, keeps her own appointments, and would be annoyed if you suggested otherwise. You've watched a friend get buried when a parent's care arrived all at once, and you'd rather learn the basics while there is nothing to coordinate.

Where they want to be

You can describe the tasks that coordinating Mom's care would involve, name two people in the family who could learn them together, and list what you'd need to find out before any of it was real.

Intermediate winI can describe what coordinating my mother's care would involve, who in the family could learn it together, and what we don't know yet.
Consumer outputA one-page starter sheet with headings: What we know now, Tasks a coordinator would carry, Who could practice together, and What we'd have to update when care begins.
Reserved for the softwareThe Family Training course teaches the operating routine with clearly labeled practice examples, runs the family through a rehearsal meeting and a concern log with a backup learner, and builds the Starter Family Care Playbook with an activation review. Sherene shows how her coordination process works and judges which skills the family has shown rather than merely attended.
Stop lineDo not create the Starter Family Care Playbook, assign a family coordinator, judge anyone's competence, or suggest that a care arrangement is needed or coming.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Waiting until stress is high to learn the tools.
  • Making documents nobody in the family can find or use.
  • Assuming one person will handle every future task.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Gather what you already know Most of what a coordinator needs on day one is information the family half knows and nobody has written down. Collecting it while Mom can simply tell you is the easiest version of this task you will ever get.
  2. Picture the tasks a coordinator would carry Care coordination sounds like a profession. Broken into its pieces, a lot of it looks like things people already do at work or at home, and some of it is genuinely new.
  3. Find a practice partner The sibling who lives closest tends to become the coordinator by default, and then the only one who knows how anything works. Learning in pairs is the simplest protection against that.
  4. Put it on one page, with a note about what would change A planning document that nobody revisits quietly goes wrong. The useful version says, on its own face, what would need checking before anyone relied on it.

  3. Lesson 3 · Manage difficult family conversations
    • Discuss workload and limits.
    • Ask for realistic commitments.
    • Do not promise to resolve entrenched conflict through a checklist.
  4. Lesson 4 · Follow through collaboratively
    • Document what was agreed.
    • Check whether commitments were completed.
    • Seek outside help when the issue exceeds the family’s or Sherene’s role.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your husband's care is mostly working, but something isn't right, and you've mentioned it twice without anything changing. Your kids ask how they can help and you say 'I've got it,' because explaining would take longer than doing it.

Where they want to be

You can state one issue as what you saw and what you're asking for, name a specific contribution to ask each relative for, and leave the conversation with the commitments written down instead of remembered.

Intermediate winI can put one concern into a clear request, ask each person in my family for something specific, and write down what was agreed.
Consumer outputA one-page conversation sheet with headings: What I noticed, What I'm asking for, What I'm asking each relative to take on, Commitments and dates, and Still unresolved.
Reserved for the softwareThe Family Advocacy course rehearses the conversation out loud, teaches listening and clarifying the response, sets up a family discussion process for disagreements, and builds the Family Advocacy and Conversation Toolkit. Sherene models her work-alongside approach, helps the family tell a care-team concern from a family one, and knows when a disagreement needs outside facilitation or a different professional.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Advocacy and Conversation Toolkit, decide whether a complaint about care is justified, assess your husband's safety, judge a provider, mediate a family conflict, or script accusations.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Carrying every responsibility yourself.
  • Letting a disagreement turn into an accusation.
  • Walking away from the conversation with nothing written down.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Pick one issue and strip it down to what you saw By the time you raise a concern, it has usually gathered a month of frustration around it. The care team can act on what you saw; they can't act on how tired you are of saying it.
  2. Turn it into one request someone can say yes to 'Please pay more attention to him' cannot be done by Friday. 'Please check his water glass at each visit and tell me by Friday if that's possible' can.
  3. Give each relative something specific to say yes to 'Let me know if you need anything' is a kind sentence that produces nothing. People say yes to a task with a name, a day, and a size they can picture.
  4. Write down what everyone agreed, and what is still open A good conversation evaporates in a week. A sheet with names and dates on it is what turns 'we talked about it' into something that happens, and it keeps the disagreements that didn't settle from quietly disappearing.
