14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your father is fine. The last time your family tried to decide something together it was a holiday menu, and it still got tense. You can see that one day the decisions will be about him, and you'd rather work out how to talk now, while nobody is tired or scared.

Where they want to be

You can describe how your family tends to handle disagreement, propose two or three ground rules for talking about your father's care, and show how a commitment or an open question would get written down.

Intermediate winI can say how my family handles disagreement today, suggest a few ground rules we might agree on, and show how we'd record what we decide.
Consumer outputA one-page draft discussion agreement with headings: How we talk now, Ground rules to propose, How we'll say a limit, How we'll record decisions and open questions, and Who else we'd ask if we got stuck.
Reserved for the softwareThe Family Advocacy course runs low-pressure practice with a hypothetical disagreement, teaches advocacy from the person's own priorities rather than from control, and helps the family turn its draft into a working discussion agreement inside the Family Advocacy and Conversation Toolkit. Sherene brings her work-alongside approach to the family conversation and recognizes when a pattern needs facilitation beyond what any checklist can do.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Advocacy and Conversation Toolkit, name anyone in the family as the future coordinator, diagnose family dynamics, mediate an existing conflict, or promise that care conversations will go smoothly.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Avoiding disagreement until a crisis forces it.
  • Treating a request for help as an admission of failure.
  • Expecting one relative to be the permanent coordinator.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Notice how your family already decides things Your family already has a way of handling disagreement; it just hasn't been named. Naming it while the stakes are a dinner menu is a lot easier than naming it in a hospital corridor.
  2. Draft ground rules everyone could live with Ground rules work when they are few, short, and sound like your family. Five rules written as things you will do beat twenty written as things you won't.
  3. Practice saying a limit and asking for something The hardest sentences in family care are 'I can't do that' and 'Would you take this on?' Saying them for the first time in a made-up situation is much easier than saying them for the first time when it counts.
  4. Put the draft agreement on one page The point of the page is not to settle anything. It is to give your family something concrete to argue with, which is a far better start than a blank table at Thanksgiving.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Mom's care has settled into a routine, and Sherene has raised the idea of stepping back from the week-to-week coordination. You want to be able to handle it. You also don't want to find out in a bad week that you can't reach anyone.

Where they want to be

You can say which tasks you believe are moving to the family and which should stay with professionals, name the kind of support you'd want to ask about, and describe the changes that would send you back for help.

Intermediate winI can say what I think my family is taking over for Mom, what support I'd want to ask about, and what would make me call for help.
Consumer outputA one-page handoff question sheet with headings: What we think we're taking over, What should stay with professionals, Support we want to ask about, Changes that would send us back for help, and Questions to settle before anything changes.
Reserved for the softwareThe Ongoing Support course works through the actual handoff: confirming which responsibilities transfer and which remain with professionals, discussing check-ins or meeting support as defined options still to be confirmed, recording re-engagement triggers, and setting a review date, all inside the Family Handoff and Ongoing Support Agreement. Sherene confirms readiness with the family, states what her scope and availability actually are, and agrees the handoff.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Handoff and Ongoing Support Agreement, declare the family ready, end or change the arrangement with Sherene, promise that any check-in or support will be available, or decide what counts as an emergency.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Ending support without anyone checking readiness.
  • Assuming someone will always be available.
  • Not knowing when it's time to ask for help again.

The prompts, one job each

  1. Sort what moves and what stays, as questions 'Taking over' is vague enough to hide a dozen tasks nobody agreed to. Writing each one as a question keeps the family from assuming something has transferred when it hasn't.
  2. Name the support you'd want to ask about Families often assume the consultant will 'still be around' and the consultant assumes the family knows what that means. Neither assumption survives the first difficult month.
  3. Describe what would send you back for help The worst time to decide whether something is serious enough to call about is while it is happening. A short list made on a calm day does that thinking for you.
  4. Write the questions to settle before anything changes This page is your side of the handoff conversation, not the handoff. It tells Sherene what the family wants, what it wonders, and what it would need to see, and leaves the agreeing to the two of you.

14 · Prompt guide strategy

What the free guide must accomplish and where it must stop. The consumer version is generated from this: open the guide.

Where they are

Your wife is healthy, and so are you. A friend's family fell apart trying to find help in the week after a fall, and you've decided you'd rather know where help lives before you need it. Nothing is wrong; you just want a map.

Where they want to be

You can describe what you'd likely manage on your own, list the kinds of help you'd want to have identified ahead of time, and name a few changes that would tell you to pick up the phone.

Intermediate winI can say what my wife and I would probably handle ourselves, what kinds of help I'd want to know about in advance, and what would tell me it's time to ask.
Consumer outputA one-page support map with headings: What we'd probably handle ourselves, Kinds of help to identify in advance, Questions to ask before relying on any service, Changes that would tell us to ask for help, and When to look at this page again.
Reserved for the softwareThe Ongoing Support course turns the map into future handoff criteria, works through the scope and availability questions a family should settle before choosing any service, keeps community and coaching distinct from urgent professional help, and records it all in the Family Handoff and Ongoing Support Agreement without implying any service is committed. Sherene explains what she offers, what she doesn't, and which professional fits which kind of problem.
Stop lineDo not create the Family Handoff and Ongoing Support Agreement, recommend or compare specific services, assess your wife's health or safety, promise availability from any professional, or suggest that care is needed or coming.
Call to actionCreate Your Free Family Care Profile · Placeholder; set to the care interview's public address before publishing.

Roadblocks the prompts get past

  • Waiting for a breakdown to start looking for contacts.
  • Expecting community support to do what professional care does.
  • Planning around one expert being endlessly available.

The prompts, one job each

  1. See what you'd probably handle yourselves Most couples would handle more than they fear and less than they assume. Sorting it on a calm day, with no one watching, is the honest way to find out which.
  2. Sketch the kinds of help worth knowing about A neighbor who drives, a church group that brings meals, a paid aide, a care consultant, and a nurse are five different kinds of help. Families get into trouble when they expect one kind to do the work of another.
  3. Write the questions to ask before relying on anyone The plan that fails is the one built around a person who turns out to be on vacation. The same five questions, asked of a neighbor and an agency alike, keep that from happening.
  4. Put the map on one page, with a date to look at it again A support map is only useful if you can find it and if it is roughly current. One page, in the drawer with the other important papers, with a date on it, does both.
